articles.summary: How easy is it to build a business after serving time in jail?
articles.body: Post-prison businesses. From the board room to a jail cell... and back again? How easy is it to re-build a career after serving time for financial offences? Riordan Maynard was CEO of mobile phone company Touchbase which he grew from a small business selling mobile phones to a multi-national company with offices in Europe, Australia, Asia, and the USA. After the financial crisis of 2008, though, the company lost hundreds of millions of pounds worth of deals and what Riordan did next landed him in a US jail for five and a half years. His experience in prison, witnessing brutal violence and struggling with his mental health, sparked an idea for a new business. Sushovan Hussain was CFO of Autonomy, founded by the late Mike Lynch. He helped the business grow into one of Britain’s biggest technology companies. But after the company was sold on, he was convicted of fraud in the US and in 2019 he was sentenced to 5 years in jail. Leaving prison and struggling with getting insurance and bank accounts inspired him to set up a new business helping ex-offendors get back into work. articles.title: Edital destina R$ 1,5 milhão para pesquisas sobre feminicídio no MA; veja requisitos | G1
articles.standfirst: O edital é voltado a professores efetivos da Uema, que podem apresentar propostas até 11 de novembro. A iniciativa prevê seis vagas para pesquisadores e 12 bolsas de iniciação científica para estudantes da universidade.
articles.summary: O edital é voltado a professores efetivos da Uema, que podem apresentar propostas até 11 de novembro. A iniciativa prevê seis vagas para pesquisadores e 12 bolsas de iniciação científica para estudantes da universidade.
articles.body:
Edital destina R$ 1,5 milhão para pesquisas sobre feminicídio no MA — Foto: Magnific.com

A Defensoria Pública do Estado do Maranhão (DPE-MA), a Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa e ao Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico do Maranhão (Fapema) e a Universidade Estadual do Maranhão (Uema) lançaram um edital para estruturar o Observatório Maranhense do Feminicídio . A iniciativa prevê R$ 1.518.400 em recursos para pesquisas sobre feminicídio no estado.

As inscrições para apresentação de propostas começaram nessa quarta-feira (28) e seguem até 11 de novembro de 2026. Podem participar professores do quadro efetivo da Uema lotados nos campi indicados no edital.

O projeto prevê a criação de cinco núcleos de pesquisa, com seis vagas para pesquisadores e 12 bolsas de iniciação científica . Os núcleos serão distribuídos entre São Luís e Região Metropolitana, Bacabal , Timon , Pinheiro e Grajaú .

Das seis vagas para pesquisadores, duas são destinadas ao Núcleo de Integração e Dados (NID), em São Luís e Região Metropolitana. As outras quatro serão distribuídas entre os núcleos regionais, com uma vaga para cada unidade.

O edital também prevê 12 bolsas de iniciação científica para estudantes de graduação da Uema. Para concorrer às bolsas, os alunos devem estar regularmente matriculados em cursos da universidade nos campi-sede dos núcleos e residir no Maranhão.

Os estudos vão abordar o feminicídio em diferentes regiões do Maranhão. Entre os recortes previstos estão a qualidade dos dados oficiais, a concentração de casos nas áreas urbanas, o acesso à rede de proteção e as dificuldades enfrentadas por mulheres de comunidades rurais, quilombolas e indígenas.

O edital também prevê pesquisas sobre a violência em regiões de fronteira entre estados e as dificuldades de acesso à Justiça e aos serviços de proteção.

As propostas devem ser submetidas entre 28 de outubro e 11 de novembro de 2026, conforme o cronograma do edital.

A etapa de análise das candidaturas e do mérito das propostas está prevista para ocorrer de 12 a 25 de novembro. O resultado preliminar deve ser divulgado em 27 de novembro, enquanto a publicação do resultado final está prevista para 4 de dezembro de 2026.

Os requisitos para participação e a documentação necessária estão descritos no edital do Observatório Maranhense do Feminicídio.

articles.title: Incêndio no Mercado Público de Arapiraca assusta comerciantes | G1
articles.standfirst: Mercado fica na Rua Teodorico Costa, no centro da cidade. Testemunhas informaram que fogo pode ter começado por causa de uma vela que estava acesa dentro do box.
articles.summary: Mercado fica na Rua Teodorico Costa, no centro da cidade. Testemunhas informaram que fogo pode ter começado por causa de uma vela que estava acesa dentro do box.
articles.body:
Comerciantes ajudam a apagar incêndio no Mercado Público de Arapiraca — Foto: Reprodução/TV Asa Branca Alagoas

Um incêndio atingiu um box do Mercado Público de Arapiraca , no Agreste de Alagoas, na manhã desta quinta-feira (29). Não houve registro de feridos. A causa do incêndio não foi confirmada.

As chamas começaram por volta das 6h. O mercado fica na Rua Teodorico Costa, no centro da cidade . Segundo testemunhas, o fogo pode ter começado por causa de uma vela que estava acesa dentro do box.

As chamas e a fumaça assustaram visitantes e permissionários que trabalham no local. De acordo com o Corpo de Bombeiros Militar (CBM), o incêndio foi combatido com água.

Em entrevista à TV Asa Branca Alagoas , o comerciante José Aparecido da Silva contou que ajudou a apagar o fogo. Segundo ele, o box onde o incêndio começou vendia produtos de religiões de matriz africana.

“Eu cheguei às 6h e já estava esse fogaréu. O fogo já estava começando a se alastrar. Demorou uns 30 minutos para apagar o incêndio. O proprietário não estava”, relatou o comerciante.

articles.title: Papais Noéis de diferentes partes do país se reúnem em Gramado | G1
articles.standfirst: Evento reúne 60 representantes de seis estados do Brasil na Serra gaúcha. Programação segue até sexta-feira (30) com atividades de integração e interação com o público nas ruas da cidade.
articles.summary: Evento reúne 60 representantes de seis estados do Brasil na Serra gaúcha. Programação segue até sexta-feira (30) com atividades de integração e interação com o público nas ruas
articles.body:
O que era para ser apenas um passeio turístico por Gramado , na Serra Gaúcha, acabou se transformando na realização de um sonho de infância para a pedagoga Roberta Rocha Guimarães, de Maceió (AL).

Ao caminhar pelo centro da cidade, ela se deparou com dezenas de participantes reunidos para o 16º Encontro Nacional de Papais Noéis , que segue até sexta-feira (30).

A visitante conta que cresceu sem viver momentos que associava ao Natal e se emocionou ao encontrar os personagens.

"Me tocou muito porque eu fui uma criança que não teve festa, que não teve memórias com pai e com mãe. A gente sempre sonha em tirar foto com o Papai Noel", relata.

Turista se emociona ao ver dezenas de Papais Noéis reunidos em Gramado: 'Memória que vou levar para a vida' — Foto: Ana Júlia Griguol /RBS TV

Ao ver o grupo reunido, a visitante não conseguiu conter as lágrimas. "A emoção foi à flor da pele. Isso me fez resgatar tudo lá atrás. É uma memória que vou levar para o resto da minha vida", afirma.

O encontro reúne 60 Papais Noéis de diferentes regiões do Brasil e chama a atenção de turistas e moradores que circulam pelas ruas da cidade . Há representantes do Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro e Paraná. A programação inclui atividades de integração entre os participantes e ações para interagir com turistas.

Papais Noéis de diferentes partes do país se reúnem em Gramado — Foto: Ana Júlia Griguol/RBS TV

Um dos Papais Noéis é Alberto José Antônio Martinho, de 72 anos , de Braço do Norte (SC), que carrega uma trajetória diferente da maioria dos participantes do encontro. Ex-mecânico de bicicletas, profissão que exerceu por quatro décadas, ele atua como Papai Noel há 30 anos ao lado da esposa, que interpreta a Mamãe Noel.

A história começou de forma inesperada. Dono de uma oficina, ele costumava receber visitas de crianças de uma creche. Com a barba comprida, passou a ser associado ao personagem pelos pequenos, que chamavam o local de "Casa do Papai Noel" . A partir dali, decidiu assumir o papel.

Segundo Alberto, a experiência mudou sua relação com o Natal. Filho de uma família com 14 irmãos, ele conta que cresceu em meio a dificuldades financeiras e sem a figura do Papai Noel presente nas comemorações.

"Na minha infância eu não tinha Natal. Era só trabalho e dificuldades", relembra.

A lembrança da infância motivou uma decisão que se mantém até hoje. Alberto diz que procura ajudar crianças e famílias durante todo o ano, distribuindo brinquedos, doces e donativos sempre que encontra alguém em situação de necessidade.

"O Papai Noel, na realidade, não tem preço, tem valores. O valor do Papai Noel é ver as pessoas felizes", conclui.

articles.title: Midterms: como funciona o sistema eleitoral americano? | G1
articles.standfirst: Votação será em 3 de novembro e vai renovar a Câmara e um terço do Senado. Entenda as regras que diferenciam o sistema eleitoral americano do brasileiro.
articles.summary: Votação será em 3 de novembro e vai renovar a Câmara e um terço do Senado. Entenda as regras que diferenciam o sistema eleitoral americano do brasileiro.
articles.body:
As eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos , conhecidas como midterms , serão realizadas em 3 de novembro. A votação renova quase todo o Congresso americano, mas segue regras diferentes das adotadas no Brasil.

▶️ Contexto: O Congresso dos Estados Unidos é renovado parcialmente a cada dois anos. Quando ocorrem na metade do mandato presidencial, essas eleições são chamadas de midterms, ou eleições de meio de mandato.

Os deputados norte-americanos têm mandatos de dois anos, enquanto os senadores, de seis.

Com isso, a cada dois anos, o país renova toda a Câmara dos Representantes e cerca de um terço do Senado.

Sendo assim, em novembro, estarão em disputa todas as 435 cadeiras da Câmara e 35 das 100 do Senado.

O sistema eleitoral dos Estados Unidos tem diferenças importantes em relação ao brasileiro. No Congresso, por exemplo, o Senado e a Câmara dos Representantes seguem regras diferentes.

No Senado, cada um dos 50 estados tem direito a duas cadeiras, independentemente do tamanho da população. Por isso, a Casa tem 100 senadores no total.

Já na Câmara dos Representantes, as 435 cadeiras são distribuídas entre os estados de acordo com a população. Cada deputado representa uma região, chamada de distrito eleitoral.

Os distritos são áreas dentro de cada estado que podem reunir cidades inteiras ou apenas parte delas.

O 11º distrito de Nova York, por exemplo, reúne apenas alguns bairros da cidade de Nova York.

Esses distritos são desenhados com base na população. Em geral, cada um deve ter um número parecido de habitantes.

Isso significa que cada deputado representa uma fatia semelhante da população dentro do estado.

Como o número de deputados de cada estado depende da população, estados mais populosos têm mais representantes na Câmara.

Local de votação em Ohio, em 6 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton

Antes das midterms, os partidos realizam eleições primárias para escolher os candidatos que vão disputar cada cargo.

Com isso, nas eleições oficiais, a disputa acaba concentrada em dois candidatos na maioria dos estados e distritos: um republicano e um democrata que venceram as primárias dos respectivos partidos.

Candidatos independentes também podem participar das eleições. No entanto, em geral, eles têm menos visibilidade e recebem menos votos.

Além disso, cada estado é responsável por apurar os próprios votos. Ao contrário do Brasil, os Estados Unidos não têm um órgão nacional como o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), responsável por coordenar as eleições em todo o país.

Em geral, a apuração começa assim que os locais de votação fecham. O horário varia de estado para estado.

Na Flórida, por exemplo, a votação termina às 19h.

Em Nova York, os eleitores têm até as 21h.

No Tennessee, o horário varia de acordo com o condado.

Com isso, os primeiros resultados devem ser divulgados ainda na noite de 3 de novembro. No entanto, pode levar dias até que seja possível saber qual partido terá o controle da Câmara e do Senado.

Em 2022, por exemplo, a disputa pela maioria da Câmara só foi definida mais de uma semana após a eleição. A demora ocorreu, entre outros fatores, porque alguns estados levam mais tempo para contar os votos enviados pelo correio.

Veja, a seguir, um guia de perguntas e respostas sobre as eleições de 2026:

O que são as midterms e por que elas têm esse nome?

Trump não está nas urnas, mas por que essa eleição é crucial para ele?

Voto pelo correio: como funciona e por que virou um dos principais temas da campanha?

A guerra dos mapas eleitorais: por que republicanos e democratas entraram nessa disputa?

1. O que são as midterms e por que elas têm esse nome?

Midterms - Eleitora preenche cédula de votação em Harrisburg, na Pensilvânia (EUA) — Foto: REUTERS/Mike Segar

As midterms são as eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos. Elas recebem esse nome porque acontecem na metade do mandato presidencial.

As últimas eleições ocorreram em 2024. Trump tomou posse em janeiro de 2025, assim como os deputados e senadores eleitos naquele ano.

Em novembro de 2026, Trump estará na metade do mandato presidencial, enquanto os deputados eleitos em 2024 e os senadores eleitos em 2020 estarão perto do fim do mandato.

Os parlamentares eleitos nas midterms tomarão posse em janeiro de 2027.

Trump não disputa a eleição, e o mandato presidencial dele termina em janeiro de 2029.

A próxima eleição presidencial será em 2028. Na mesma data, haverá eleições para renovar todas as cadeiras da Câmara dos Representantes e cerca de um terço das vagas do Senado.

A eleição está marcada para 3 de novembro . No entanto, a votação antecipada já começou em alguns estados, e parte dos eleitores já votou pelo correio.

3. Trump não está nas urnas, mas por que essa eleição é crucial para ele?

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, discursa em um comício de campanha em apoio ao candidato republicano ao Senado, Mike Collins, e ao candidato a governador, Rick Jackson, em Dalton, Geórgia, EUA, em 16 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

Nas eleições de 2024, o Partido Republicano, o mesmo de Trump, conquistou a maioria das cadeiras da Câmara e do Senado. Com isso, a legenda passou a controlar a pauta e as votações nas duas Casas.

Isso permitiu que Trump aprovasse pautas importantes para o governo dele. Ainda assim, ele enfrentou dificuldades, já que a maioria republicana é pequena e alguns parlamentares do partido contrariaram o presidente em votações.

Agora, Trump quer manter a maioria para continuar tendo apoio no Congresso. Uma derrota na Câmara, no Senado ou em ambas as Casas poderia dificultar a aprovação de projetos do presidente e abrir espaço para os parlamentares barrarem ações do governo.

4. Desaprovação recorde: como Trump chega às midterms?

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, discursa na Assembleia Geral da ONU, em 22 de setembro de 2026 — Foto: Mike Segar/Reuters

Uma pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos divulgada no dia 19 de outubro apontou que 66% dos americanos desaprovam o governo de Donald Trump . O índice está entre os mais altos da série histórica para os dois mandatos do presidente.

Além disso, o levantamento apontou que 31% aprovam o governo Trump. O índice é o mais baixo registrado por uma pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos nos dois mandatos do republicano e está abaixo do registrado pelo antecessor dele, Joe Biden.

Segundo a pesquisa, a insatisfação dos eleitores está ligada principalmente à forma como Trump conduz a economia e ao alto custo de vida nos Estados Unidos.

Foto do Senado dos EUA, no Capitólio, em Washington, na madrugada de terça-feira, 8 de novembro de 2022 — Foto: J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Pesquisas e projeções recentes indicam que os democratas podem conquistar a maioria do Senado nas eleições de novembro.

Atualmente, os republicanos têm 53 cadeiras na Casa, enquanto os democratas contam com 47 senadores, incluindo dois independentes que costumam votar junto com o partido. As projeções indicam que esse cenário pode mudar a partir de 2027. Veja a seguir.

7. Voto pelo correio: como funciona e por que virou um dos principais temas da campanha?

Funcionários eleitorais separam cédulas de voto por correio no escritório do Supervisor de Eleições do Condado de Miami-Dade para as eleições primárias da Flórida, em 18 de agosto de 2026 — Foto: AP Photo/Lynne Sladky

Todos os 50 estados permitem alguma forma de votação pelo correio. Desses, 37 estados e Washington, D.C., permitem que os eleitores solicitem uma cédula sem apresentar justificativa, segundo levantamento do Centro para Inovação e Pesquisa Eleitoral.

As regras variam de estado para estado. De forma geral, os eleitores que escolhem essa modalidade recebem a cédula pelo correio, preenchem o documento e o enviam de volta dentro do prazo estabelecido.

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, tem defendido restrições ao voto pelo correio e afirma que o sistema é suscetível a fraudes.

Em março, ele assinou um decreto para endurecer as regras de votação por correspondência e ampliar a verificação da cidadania dos eleitores.

A medida prevê a criação de uma lista federal de cidadãos aptos a votar pelo correio, elaborada pelo Serviço de Cidadania e Imigração dos EUA e pela Administração da Seguridade Social.

Pelo decreto, as cédulas enviadas pelo correio só poderiam ser entregues a pessoas incluídas nesse cadastro.

Trump afirma que a medida visa impedir fraudes e que pessoas sem cidadania americana votem nos Estados Unidos.

Alguns estados e organizações de defesa do direito ao voto contestaram judicialmente as novas regras. Eles argumentam que a Constituição dos EUA atribui aos estados e ao Congresso, e não ao presidente, o poder de definir as regras eleitorais.

Em setembro, a Suprema Corte manteve o bloqueio a uma regra do Serviço Postal dos EUA que implementaria parte do decreto de Trump antes das eleições de novembro.

A norma exigiria que os estados enviassem listas de eleitores aptos a votar pelo correio e que os envelopes das cédulas tivessem códigos de barras específicos.

Com isso, o órgão poderia recusar o envio de cédulas que não cumprissem essas exigências.

8. A guerra dos mapas eleitorais: por que republicanos e democratas entraram nessa disputa?

presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, responde a perguntas durante o anúncio do plano de uma empresa de Minnesota para construir uma siderúrgica de US$ 15 bilhões em Iowa, no Salão Oval da Casa Branca, em Washington, DC, EUA, em 28 de setembro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

Para evitar perder o controle da Câmara, Trump sugeriu que os republicanos apoiassem o redesenho dos distritos eleitorais nos estados. A estratégia era criar mapas mais favoráveis ao partido.

A ofensiva de Trump começou pelo Texas. O estado tem o segundo maior número de deputados do país e é um importante reduto republicano.

A proposta foi aprovada no estado em agosto de 2025 e já está em vigor. Com o novo desenho, a expectativa é que os republicanos ganhem vantagem ao redistribuir eleitores e reduzir o número de distritos em que os democratas tinham vantagem.

A estratégia, no entanto, gerou reação. Três meses depois, a Califórnia decidiu redesenhar o próprio mapa para favorecer os democratas. Com isso, a expectativa é que o partido conquiste cinco cadeiras atualmente ocupadas por republicanos.

Mas a disputa continuou. Os republicanos conseguiram redesenhar os mapas de outros seis estados: Alabama, Flórida, Louisiana, Carolina do Norte, Ohio e Tennessee.

Em Utah, uma decisão judicial também levou à criação de um distrito eleitoral com tendência democrata em Salt Lake City.

articles.title: Special Ed Teacher Who Rented Hotel Rooms With Her Student Gets Six Months, and She Can Serve It at Home
articles.summary: Former special education teacher at Tartan High School has been sentenced to six months for a sexual relationship with a student who was 18 years old and sti...
articles.body:
Former special education teacher at Tartan High School has been sentenced to six months for a sexual relationship with a student who was 18 years old and still in her class.

Ann Margaret Bacon, 27, of Hastings, got her sentence on Monday in Ramsey County District Court after pleading guilty in September to criminal sexual conduct in the third degree involving a prohibited occupational relationship.

Judge Thomas Gilligan Jr. ordered 180 days with two years of supervised probation, the St. Paul Pioneer Press reported . Bacon got credit for two days already served and may serve the rest on electronic home monitoring.

He agreed to a plea bargain in which prosecutors and the defense jointly requested a downward departure from the sentencing guidelines. The agreement asked for a gross misdemeanor conviction and no more than 364 days in jail. Judge Gilligan granted the departure because Bacon was willing to comply with probation.

Educators cannot have a sexual relationship with their students in Minnesota, even if the student is 18 or older, KARE 11 reported at the time Bacon was charged.

According to criminal allegations, Bacon rented a room in a Vadnais Heights hotel on May 8, June 4, June 11, and July 4, 2023, staying one night each time. Bacon rented a room a "handful" of times to be intimate with the student because she was living with her parents until she found an apartment in July, KSTP reported.

In an interview with police on February 8, 2024, Bacon denied the relationship, stating that it started only after the student graduated. She later changed her story after investigators showed her pictures of the two taken May 8 in the hotel. She admitted that the relationship started when the student was still one of her students, about a month before his graduation, the Pioneer Press reported , citing the complaint.

The student, who admitted that he was in Bacon's class during his senior year, also stated to police that they did not have sex until July 2023, after he graduated.

Witnesses stated that Bacon bought alcohol for the student and other minors. One witness described a video on the student's phone from May 2023, showing Bacon, the student and some friends drinking in a hotel room, according to the Pioneer Press .

Bacon denied buying alcohol for minors. She admitted receiving a $40 Venmo payment on June 21, 2023, with the note "liqq," but said she could not recall who sent it and what it was for, FOX 9 reported, citing the complaint.

The case emerged due to people close to the student. A witness and her friend first raised concerns with the school in July 2023, but they had no evidence at the time. Later, another witness stated to police that there were sexually explicit messages and nude photos of Bacon and the student on his phone, according to KSTP.

School records revealed that a tipster reported the allegations on July 9, 2023. Two days later, the principal called Bacon, who denied any inappropriate interactions with students. The complaint states that no further action was taken and administrators did not make a mandatory report to the police, the Pioneer Press reported.

Ty Thompson, the district's assistant superintendent of secondary schools, told the Pioneer Press in 2024 that there "were no facts to support a reasonable belief of neglect or abuse" at that time.

The witness came forward again in February 2024, worrying that Bacon was still teaching and could access vulnerable students. Administrators and a school resource officer were informed of the report on February 6, 2024, FOX 9 reported, and the police opened an investigation. Prosecutors charged Bacon, then 24, with felony criminal sexual conduct in the third degree six days later.

Bacon resigned the same day police interviewed her. She was hired as a special education teacher in August 2022 after working at Tartan as a paraprofessional the previous school year. She also served as a varsity assistant for the dance team.

Tartan High School is in Oakdale and belongs to Independent School District 622, which serves North St. Paul, Maplewood, and Oakdale.

articles.title: Russia’s alleged sabotage campaign in Europe raises fears of escalation
articles.summary: From drone incursions to an alleged campaign of assassinations, Russia is feared to be pressing a shadow war.
articles.body:
Russia appears to have escalated its shadow war in Europe this year.

European officials have alleged that Russian fighter planes have veered inside Polish, Lithuanian and Estonian airspace, testing reaction times. Suspected Russian drones have been downed over Poland, Finland and the Baltic states.

And Moscow has been accused of bringing trouble to the Black Sea.

In two separate operations in October, Ukraine accused Russia of using aerial and surface drones to sink four cargo ships just outside the territorial waters of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member, in an apparent warning that Ukraine’s grain exports through NATO territorial waters may not be safe for long.

Russia and Belarus have also been accused of trying to destabilise the Baltic states by making their borders appear fluid.

“Masked and most likely armed individuals on the Belarus side of the border escorted and attempted to push groups of illegal migrants into Latvia,” Ieva Cesniece, Latvia’s ambassador to Greece, told Al Jazeera. “Those individuals expressed threats to Latvian soldiers and border guards. On the same day in a separate incident, masked individuals crossed into Latvian territory and carried out deliberate sabotage. Bborder infrastructure was damaged, and surveillance equipment was removed.”

Latvian media have reported that asylum seekers and undocumented migrants who tried to run back from the Latvian border were rounded up by Belarusian authorities and pushed towards Latvia again.

Cesniece drew a direct link between the Russian war in Ukraine and its shadow war in Europe.

“The weaker Russia appears in Ukraine, the more it tests our resilience, trying to weaken NATO and EU resolve and support for Ukraine,” she said.

As European governments warned of an imminent escalation of a Russian shadow war on the continent, experts said the bloc needs to do more to deter Russia as well as defend itself.

“Protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening intelligence services and preventing attacks are essential, but deterrence is about more than preventing the next incident,” said Olena Tregub, cofounder and head of Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission. “It is about convincing your adversary that continuing these operations will become too costly. And I’m not sure Russia currently sees those costs as sufficiently high.”

As an expert on following money trails, she believes European governments have not done enough to identify the networks behind operations, expose the command structures, disrupt their financing and logistics, and impose consequences.

Meanwhile, Russia’s war is going badly on the ground.

Two Ukrainian counteroffensives have blunted Moscow’s main thrust to capture the eastern region of Donetsk and in effect have deprived it of any territorial gains this year.

Since a failed August operation to blow up cargo planes at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, which was later verified by the European Commission as a Russian operation, warnings of further escalation have multiplied.

Czech spy chief Michal Koudelka warned in September that Russia might attempt a military attack on a NATO member in “months, not years”.

Days later, Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova openly declared that European defence industries supplying Ukraine were legitimate targets for Moscow.

“Russia does not necessarily distinguish between the military capabilities Ukraine uses on the battlefield and the European infrastructure that makes those capabilities possible,” Tregub told Al Jazeera.

“From Moscow’s perspective, a factory producing military equipment for Ukraine, a logistics hub transporting that equipment or a company providing critical technology can all become potential targets of disruption.”

This month, representatives of five EU intelligence agencies told the Financial Times that Russia was seeking to “kill” European defence bosses and target their supply chains.

That followed a report from a German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, that Russia had planted incendiary devices in the offices of defence companies Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing in Munich. It also followed a report on the Politico news site in which EU security officials said Russia was planning to move beyond messaging and claim lives on European soil.

European officials have spoken of strengthening the resilience of their data centres, telecommunications, and other vulnerable networks and industries, but they have not spoken of retaliation.

From the Ukrainian point of view, though, Europe has been slow to see sabotage, manned and unmanned military operations, cyberattacks and information warfare as the early stages of a multidimensional war with Russia, and that failure of perception is itself a weakness.

“Where will he stop if he is currently testing all these drones against European countries, even NATO countries?” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked journalists on October 16, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin. “They are not talking about it very loudly yet. They don’t want escalation, … but you will talk very loudly when there are ballistic and cruise missiles and also thousands of drones.”

“Ukrainians don’t know about any war in Ukraine. They know about war in Europe,” said Oleksandr Danylyuk, a long-serving adviser to the Ukrainian Ministries of Defence and Foreign Affairs and now a Russian warfare expert with the Royal United Services Institute.

Like Zelenskyy and Tregub, he believes the lack of retaliation to its apparent hybrid war encourages Russia.

“Russians are limited right now only by their capabilities because they do whatever they want. There is no reaction,” he said.

He said he believes NATO needs to place more forward troops in the Baltic states to create “deterrence by denial” and to strengthen Ukraine.

Minna Alander, a leading European researcher in security and defence with the Center for European Policy Analysis, said denying Russians travel visas, carrying out retaliatory cyberattacks, further interdicting the Russian oil fleet and sanctioning Chinese suppliers of defence goods to Russia were all realistic retaliations Europe could impose immediately.

Danylyuk said money remains the most potent tool of deterrence.

“The most direct way to punish Russia is to actually increase support to Ukraine,” he told Al Jazeera. “Each time we detect Russian intelligence operations in Europe, we will increase combined support of Ukraine [maybe] 10 percent, 20 percent.”

Yet Ukraine’s allies are signalling the opposite, he observed.

The United States withdrew its military and financial support in January 2025 and recently placed the dependability of its satellite services in doubt . In France and Germany, the governments trail opposition leaders who want to stop aid to Ukraine.

Ukraine has performed better than many expected.

Since 2023, it has designed and built its own weapons and developed its own strategy to halt the Russian advance. It has punished Russia by striking oil installations and weapons factories deep inside its territory.

To reverse the tide of the war and reclaim its occupied territories, it is asking for more money, and it is asking it from the people providing the vast majority of it – Europe.

“Next year, the war will cost 155 billion euros [$170bn]), and we need at least 70 billion euros [$80bn] more from you,” Zelenskyy told the European Council on October 16.

“We could double or even triple the production of drones,” he said. “Just imagine how much more pressure we could put on Russia if we could do two or three times more.”

articles.title: Roof repairs approved to tackle leaks at Yorkshire Museum
articles.summary: Regular leaks threaten to damage historic artefacts at the Yorkshire Museum, a senior curator warns.
articles.body:
Roof repairs at a Grade I listed museum have been approved in a bid to tackle significant and regular leaks which it is feared could eventually lead to historic items being damaged.

The Yorkshire Museum in York's Museum Gardens has seen several near misses, with leaks threatening to affect artefacts and fossils.

Senior curator Dr Andrew Woods said the museum was closing its galleries five times a year on average due to major leaks, which were preventing investment.

The repairs are set to take place over the next two years, following a £2m funding grant from Arts Council England.

The museum, which was completed in 1830, houses a number of Iron Age, Roman, Viking and Medieval artefacts and prehistoric remains, including dinosaur bones.

In the last three years, one leak had led to a pool of water forming on top of a cabinet housing Iron Age artefacts, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

Meanwhile, water had also been found running down the back of a case containing a Jurassic Ichthyosaur specimen and dripping into a cabinet full of Roman burial finds.

Woods said it was mainly down to luck that there had not been more damage to the museum's collections.

"There are galleries and spaces within the museum where we cannot put our most important or sensitive collections," he said.

"While we have a strong connection, it can be enhanced by loaning objects from other institutions.

"But there are galleries within the museum where this is not possible because the water risk is too high.

"Without confidence to invest in our permanent galleries, we are missing out on up to 75,000 visitors per annum - this would equate to the loss of potential annual revenue in excess of £500,000."

Woods said this would threaten the financial viability of the museum over the long term.

The first phase of repairs funded by the Arts Council grant is set to focus on the roof above the museum's Tempest Anderson hall and its main entrances.

Kathryn Blacker, York Museums Trust's chief executive, said the funding would help address some essential building works, improve the experience for visitors and ensure the museum remained sustainable.

articles.title: Too poor to hire a crew, Texas farmer Jackson Ellis and five sons learned oilfield work, then drilled five wells that, by 1949, brought in $5,000 a month
articles.summary: Discover how Jackson Ellis and his five sons turned their Texas farm into a successful oil operation by drilling wells, overcoming financial hurdles, and becoming self-reliant during the post-World War II oil boom.
articles.body: In the years after World War II, drilling for oil could be difficult for families who lacked capital. A family seeking more than a standard royalty often had to finance drilling itself or give a large share of the proceeds to someone who could pay for the rig and crew, because equipment and labour were expensive. Jackson Ellis, a Texas farmer with little spare cash, chose to learn the work rather than hire an outside crew.A family turned drilling crewEllis could not afford to hire a drilling crew, so he and five of his sons took on the work themselves and learned to operate the rig. A sixth and youngest son helped as a water boy, according to a 1949 account in TIME. On a professional rig, drilling machinery, derrick work and pipe handling require different skills. The family had to learn these tasks while working around heavy pipe, steel wire and machinery, all of which posed serious risks. The attempt succeeded. The family dug five wells, and by 1949 were making around $5,000 a month. That says it all. How a simple agricultural family evolved into a tiny oil operation. It didn't cost a bunch to get going. It took labour already under the same roof.Why family labour was importantA hired drilling crew had to be paid whether or not a well produced oil, so a dry well could be particularly costly for a small operator. By learning the work and drilling with family members, Ellis reduced the need to pay an outside crew, although the family's labour still involved substantial time, effort and physical risk. The arrangement reduced the cash needed to begin drilling, but it did not eliminate the possibility of losing money on an unsuccessful well.Small independent operators played an important role in Texas oil development, but the Ellis family's approach was distinct. The family worked its own property and relied on its own labour rather than depending entirely on an outside drilling crew. This reduced its initial cash requirements but did not eliminate the financial risks of drilling. Dry wells could consume time and money without producing revenue, making the reported success of five wells notable.What $5,000 a month meant At $5,000 a month, the reported income amounted to $60,000 a year in 1949. Adjusted for inflation, $5,000 a month in 1949 would be worth roughly $67,000 a month in 2026 dollars. That would have made the family's oil operation highly lucrative, although the historical account does not explain precisely which operating expenses were deducted. The figure should therefore not automatically be treated as net profit after equipment, fuel, repairs and other costs.The family was operating during a period of rapid oil development in West Texas. The Texas Almanack lists Kelly Snyder among the significant oil discoveries of 1948 and the Cogdell area among the discoveries of 1949. The Texas State Historical Association records that development of the combined Kelly Snyder field accelerated during 1949, attracting additional operators and drilling activity. This wider boom provided the regional context for the Ellis family's venture.Today, Texas oil and gas operators must meet regulatory requirements, including filing an organisation report with the Railroad Commission of Texas, obtaining the required drilling permit and maintaining the financial assurance required for their operations. The right to drill also depends on mineral ownership and lease rights. Requirements vary by operation, so the Commission's official guidance on regulatory requirements should be consulted. Ellis's story illustrates how learning the work and using family labour reduced the need for an outside crew, but it is not a general guide to modern drilling.Jackson Ellis and his sons addressed their lack of money for a drilling crew by learning the work themselves. By 1949, they had drilled five shallow wells on their property and were reportedly bringing in about $5,000 a month. Their experience shows how family labour and secondhand equipment helped one landowner take advantage of an oil opportunity, while the risks of drilling remained.You use AI every day. articles.title: For more than 15 years, eight descendants negotiated the fate of inherited land along the Maryland-Delaware border; a conservation deal has now permanently protected 181 acres of forest and wetlands across two states
articles.summary: A conservation effort spanning more than 15 years has secured 181 acres of forests, wetlands and waterways along the Nanticoke River and Wright Creek,
articles.body: A conservation effort spanning more than 15 years has secured 181 acres of forests, wetlands and waterways along the Nanticoke River and Wright Creek, preserving ecologically significant land across Maryland and Delaware. The project, announced by the Nanticoke River Watershed Conservancy and Chesapeake Conservancy, brings together multiple generations of the Porter family, state conservation agencies and federal partners to protect the landscape from future development. The newly established Henry F. Porter Preserve in Delaware and the adjacent Porter Tract in Maryland form part of a wider effort to safeguard the Chesapeake Bay watershed, where forests, tidal creeks and wetlands support wildlife and help maintain the health of connected waterways.A family inheritance becomes a conservation priorityThe project began more than 15 years ago, when the Nanticoke River Watershed Conservancy started working with eight descendants of Henry F. Porter to secure the future of their inherited property. Deeds and successive inheritances dating back to the mid-19th century complicated negotiations, requiring years of coordination among family members and conservation organisations.Porter purchased the land in 1950. To honour his legacy, the protected areas have been named after him, with the Delaware property becoming the Henry F. Porter Preserve and the Maryland parcel joining the state’s Chesapeake Forest Lands system.Chesapeake Conservancy subsequently helped advance the acquisition, purchasing the land temporarily while arrangements were made to transfer it into long-term conservation ownership. The initial acquisition comprised approximately 138 acres in Delaware and 39 acres in Maryland. The family later worked with the conservation organisations to protect an additional four wooded acres along Wright Creek.How the 181 acres will be protectedThe conservation arrangement divides the land between the two states, with different agencies overseeing its long-term protection. In Maryland, the 39-acre tract was acquired by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources using Program Open Space funding. It has been incorporated into Chesapeake Forest Lands, a network spanning more than 75,000 acres across six Maryland counties. The property will be managed as a sustainable forest and is leased to a private hunting club.In Delaware, the 142-acre preserve has been transferred to the Nanticoke River Watershed Conservancy. A conservation easement held jointly by the US Navy and the Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control restricts future development to protect the land’s conservation value.Funding for the Delaware easement came through the state’s Open Space Program and the Department of Defense’s Readiness and Environmental Protection Integration (REPI) programme. REPI supports partnerships that protect land around military installations and testing areas, helping prevent incompatible development while preserving environmental resources. The preserve borders other protected areas, including the Nanticoke Wildlife Area and Pete Gum Preserve near Seaford, Delaware. Plans also include improving existing logging trails to make the property more accessible for hiking and nature study.A wider impact on the Chesapeake Bay watershedBeyond protecting the property itself, the agreement strengthens a network of conserved landscapes in a region facing increasing development pressure. The Nanticoke watershed extends across roughly 725,000 acres and contains extensive tidal wetlands, forests and habitats for migratory birds and other wildlife.Local reporting by WBOC highlighted the project’s importance for water quality, particularly because forests and wetlands help limit sediment entering waterways. That matters for the wider Chesapeake Bay ecosystem, where changes in land use can affect aquatic habitats and the species that depend on them. The Nanticoke also supports important fish populations, including Atlantic sturgeon in its connected waterways.The project is also significant for its cross-border approach. Conservation officials have identified the need to protect connected habitats rather than isolated parcels, allowing wildlife to move through larger stretches of natural land while helping maintain ecological resilience. Chesapeake Conservancy has helped protect 26 properties covering 3,466 acres in the Nanticoke watershed with support from Mt. Cuba Center. The organisation has also identified more than 1,000 additional acres in the Mid-Atlantic Flyway that could offer substantial conservation benefits if protected.The Henry F. Porter Preserve represents a long-term investment in that broader effort, combining family stewardship, public funding and conservation partnerships to keep a landscape of forests and wetlands intact for future generations.As officials consider further opportunities to connect protected areas, the project offers an example of how sustained negotiations and cooperation between neighbouring states can deliver lasting environmental benefits.You use AI every day. articles.title: Europe’s wealth gap: Older households eight times richer than young ones
articles.summary: As protests over living costs and programme cuts spread across Europe, under-35s hold 2.8%t of household wealth.
articles.body:
Student protests that began in September in France have spread to more than 11 European countries as anger rises over high rents and fuel prices and cuts to public services.

Many young protesters said they no longer expect to be better off than their parents, and household wealth data show a wide gap between generations.

Across the eurozone and two other European countries, households headed by someone under 35 have a median net wealth of about 25,000 euros ($27,870) while those headed by 55- to 64-year-olds are worth about 208,000 euros ($231,882), more than eight times as much, according to the European Central Bank’s (ECB’s) 2023 Household Finance and Consumption Survey.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera compares wealth by age groups across 22 European countries and looks at how much more expensive life has become since 2000.

The Household Finance and Consumption Survey, run by the ECB and national central banks since 2010, tracks household wealth and debt in the eurozone, the Czech Republic and Hungary.

It measures net wealth, which includes property, cars, valuables and savings, minus debts. Under-35s hold just 2.8 percent of all household wealth in the 22 countries while 55- to 64-year-olds hold the largest share at 24 percent.

In Finland, under-35s hold 0.8 percent of household wealth, the lowest share of any country surveyed, while over-55s hold more than 71 percent. Young people’s shares are also small in Ireland (1.4 percent), Austria (1.6 percent), Greece (1.8 percent) and Germany (2 percent).

Rising housing costs mean many young people cannot afford what their parents or grandparents could.

Wealth is more evenly spread in Central and Eastern Europe. In Lithuania, under-35s hold 13.2 percent, against 15.9 percent for 55- to 64-year-olds. Their share is 12.3 percent in Croatia, 10.1 percent in Slovakia and 9.8 percent in Estonia. Malta, at 11.1 percent, is the exception outside the two regions.

The graphic below shows how household wealth is split between age groups in each country surveyed.

“What we’ve seen is actually a very strong increase in housing prices both in terms of the rental market as well as the ownership market,” Evelyn Astor of the European Social Observatory told Al Jazeera’s Counting the Cost programme.

“All of this is also reinforcing a sense of inequality because ultimately ordinary families are struggling to pay their rents or be able to purchase their homes whereas wealthy people with capital are able to make rather significant investments in the European housing market,” she said.

How much more expensive is it than 2000?

Prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, energy, transport and household bills, have risen by 67.2 percent in the eurozone, Hungary and the Czech Republic since 2000.

Of the countries in our chart, Hungary has seen the steepest rise with prices more than tripling, according to Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.

The chart below shows how consumer prices have changed in each country since 2000 with prices in 2000 set at 100 on the index.

Eastern European countries have seen the sharpest increases – particularly since 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began – because many relied heavily on Russian energy supplies.

Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average until 2022 when annual inflation in the EU hit 9.2 percent.

The surge was driven mainly by energy costs. Inflation has since eased, but the price rises of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine have not reversed.

articles.title: What qualifies as a planet?  Icy object beyond Pluto reignites debate
articles.summary: For years, Pluto held a place among the solar system’s nine planets, until its status changed in 2006.
articles.body: For years, Pluto held a place among the solar system’s nine planets, until its status changed in 2006. Now, a newly discovered icy object lurking beyond Pluto has reignited interest in the distant worlds at the edge of our solar system and the question of what qualifies as a planet.Named 2026 ED138, the object was detected using the Vera C Rubin Observatory in Chile, but further observations are needed to confirm whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet. The discovery was announced at a scientific meeting in Spokane, Washington.Researchers estimate that 2026 ED138 is between 600 and 1,500 km wide and orbits the Sun at a distance roughly 46 times that between Earth and the Sun. Pluto, by comparison, orbits at an average distance of about 40 times the Earth-Sun distance.If confirmed as a dwarf planet, 2026 ED138 would join five objects currently recognised in that category by the International Astronomical Union (IAU): Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake and Ceres. While Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake orbit beyond Neptune, Ceres is located in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.What qualifies as a dwarf planet?Astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard & Smithsonian, who first spotted 2026 ED138, told Reuters that the discovery highlights the potential for further findings with the Rubin Observatory and other telescopes.As per the information available, scientists still need to establish the object's actual size. Current observations capture sunlight reflected from its surface, making it difficult to distinguish between a smaller, highly reflective object and a larger, less reflective one. Observations using Chile's Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), which can detect light emitted by the object itself, could help researchers measure its size more accurately.To qualify as a dwarf planet, an object must have enough mass for its own gravity to pull it into a nearly round shape. Although 2026 ED138 appears to meet this requirement, further observations are needed to confirm its classification.Pluto was reclassified from the solar system's ninth planet to a dwarf planet by the IAU in 2006 because it did not meet the organisation's formal definition of a planet. Like Pluto, 2026 ED138 lies in a cold region beyond Neptune populated by icy bodies.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: North Korea fires missiles as row over landmine blast intensifies
articles.summary: Seoul accuses Pyongyang of causing a landmine explosion that injured three of its soldiers, an accusation North denies.
articles.body:
North Korea has fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), less than a week after Seoul proposed talks over a growing border dispute.

The missiles were launched at about 12:30pm (03:30 GMT) on Thursday from an area around Wonsan on North Korea’s eastern coast, the JCS said in a statement.

Japan’s Defence Ministry separately confirmed the launch of what it said could be a ballistic missile that fell outside the country’s Exclusive Economic Zone, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported.

The launch comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified border between the two Koreas, on September 21.

A joint South Korea-United Nations investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago,with Seoul calling for an apology.

Pyongyang rejected the finding, sending a letter to the UN Security Council (UNSC) this week accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion.

The North Korean permanent representative to the UN, Kim Song, wrote about the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence.

Song told the UNSC that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”.

Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, labelled South Korean demands for an apology as “despicable” while separately rejecting an offer of medical equipment from Seoul.

South Korea has proposed military talks with its neighbour in a bid to calm the situation.

Seoul said last Friday that it had invited Pyongyang to discuss restoring communication channels. The offer was made as military activity on the border increases.

It remains unclear whether North Korea would agree to talks. Leader Kim has taken a hardline approach towards Seoul and suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years.

The ratcheting tensions come as United States President Donald Trump’s recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that US ally Seoul could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.

Pyongyang launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim this year.

articles.title: El Salvador pledges more than 2,000 soldiers as Haiti delays elections
articles.summary: El Salvador troops to support rescue mission to find four UN-backed soldiers who disappeared after ambush.
articles.body:
El Salvador plans to send more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti to search for four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians and fight armed gangs, as the Caribbean country postpones its elections again.

El Salvador ‘s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the deployment on Wednesday, the same day Haiti’s electoral authorities moved the first round of presidential and parliamentary elections from December 13 to July 18, 2027.

The delay is another setback to restoring elected government in a country where gang violence has made preparations for voting dangerous.

The four Salvadorans disappeared on October 18 after armed men ambushed their vehicle in Croix-des-Bouquets, east of the capital, Port-au-Prince.

They were serving with an international security mission supporting Haitian police.

President Nayib Bukele has already sent troops to help find them.

In an October 21 post on X, written in Haitian Creole, he threatened to destroy Haiti’s gangs if they did not release the missing personnel.

Bukele spoke by telephone with Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime on Wednesday.

Fils-Aime’s office said they had agreed to strengthen cooperation on rescue efforts and security operations.

It remains unclear whether the additional Salvadoran troops will join the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force, a multinational mission assisting Haitian police against gangs, or operate separately.

Foreign troops have served in Haiti under UN-backed security arrangements since 2024, partly to create safer conditions for elections.

Haiti’s nine-member Provisional Electoral Council, which organises elections, also scheduled a second round of voting and local polls for October 4, 2027.

It extended deadlines for candidates to register and introduced online voter registration.

Fewer than 900,000 people had registered by Wednesday, the Miami Herald reported, out of 6.5 million Haitians holding the identification cards needed to enrol.

Gang-controlled roads make it difficult to reach registration centres, while violence has forced many people from their homes.

Haiti has held no elections since 2016 and its last president, Jovenel Moise , was assassinated in 2021. Successive transitional authorities have delayed a return to voting, citing insecurity.

An international food security assessment released on Wednesday found that 5.94 million Haitians face acute hunger, including 1.8 million in emergency conditions, as violence disrupts farming and food deliveries.

The number facing acute hunger is projected to rise to 6.35 million by mid-2027.

articles.title: ​Richard Sackler and his wife tried to stop the sale of their Connecticut mansion, pledged toward Purdue Pharma's $7.4 billion opioid settlement; on October 28, a bankruptcy judge rejected both requests
articles.summary: A grand Greenwich residence is rarely the kind of place one expects to find at the centre of a bankruptcy dispute.
articles.body: A grand Greenwich residence is rarely the kind of place one expects to find at the centre of a bankruptcy dispute. Yet Richard Sackler and Lin Gao’s Connecticut mansion has become one of the most closely watched properties in the continuing financial fallout from Purdue Pharma and the US opioid crisis. The home at 60 Field Point Circle is now tied to the Sackler family’s obligations under a $7.4 billion settlement involving opioid claimants. On October 28, US Bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane rejected efforts by Sackler and Gao to prevent the property from being sold, keeping the mansion within the pool of assets being used to fund the settlement. Reuters reports that Lane had previously determined the Greenwich residence was among the assets pledged by Sackler family members as collateral for their commitments under the agreement.A home at the centre of a larger reckoningThe property dispute is only one part of a much broader reckoning involving the family that once owned Purdue Pharma. The pharmaceutical company became one of the most recognisable names in the opioid crisis through its aggressive marketing of OxyContin, a prescription painkiller that became central to the national addiction epidemic.Purdue's bankruptcy followed tens of thousands of lawsuits brought by states, municipalities and other parties over the company's role in the crisis. The resulting settlement requires the Sackler family to provide much of the funding, with a substantial portion directed towards state and local governments. According to Reuters, the Greenwich mansion was transferred from one Sackler family trust to another as part of efforts to free up money for a $62 million settlement payment.The court says the sale must continueSackler and Gao sought to challenge the earlier ruling concerning the property and asked the court to temporarily stop any sale. Both requests were rejected by Lane during Wednesday's hearing. The judge's decision means the property remains subject to the process of converting pledged assets into funds for the settlement. Reuters reports that Lane viewed the couple's attempts to interfere with the sale as inconsistent with the obligations they had undertaken as part of the settlement arrangements.The ruling does not require Sackler and Gao to immediately leave the residence. However, the court left open the possibility of further action if the dispute continues, including sanctions or measures affecting their occupancy.Selling a house that is still occupiedThe practical side of selling the mansion presents another complication. Gao and her children continue to live at the property, while the residence also contains artwork that forms part of the assets being considered for sale. Reuters reports that the trust overseeing the sale has indicated that the family's continued presence in the home has made the process more difficult. Determining how the residence and its contents can be prepared for sale adds another layer to an already complicated bankruptcy proceeding. Sackler and Gao's lawyers have said they plan to appeal the earlier decision that allowed the property sale to proceed.The Sackler fortune under scrutinyThe dispute also brings renewed attention to Richard Sackler's role at Purdue Pharma. Now 81, he served as the company's president and chairman during its aggressive promotion of OxyContin. Purdue Pharma pleaded guilty twice to deceptive marketing of the drug. Members of the Sackler family, however, were not personally charged with misconduct in connection with those cases.The family's financial settlement has nevertheless placed its assets under sustained scrutiny, turning properties and other holdings associated with the Sackler fortune into potential sources of compensation.What happens to the Greenwich MansionFor now, the Field Point Circle property remains occupied, but its status has changed dramatically. Rather than simply being a private family residence, it has become part of a court-supervised effort to fulfil financial commitments arising from Purdue Pharma's bankruptcy. Reuters notes that Sackler also owns four other homes, including a primary residence in Florida. The Connecticut mansion, meanwhile, remains caught between private ownership, family occupancy and the demands of a settlement designed to address the enormous human and financial consequences of the opioid crisis.Its eventual sale could therefore represent more than a real-estate transaction. It would mark another step in converting the wealth accumulated during Purdue Pharma's rise into funds connected to the aftermath of America's opioid epidemic.​Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and RealtorYou use AI every day. articles.title: European Union backtracks on Canada becoming ‘associate member’
articles.summary: Several European leaders reportedly pushed for the term to be removed from a joint draft Canada-EU statement.
articles.body:
The European Union has dropped the idea that Canada should become an “associate member” of the bloc, according to media reports.

In a joint draft Canada-EU statement, the terms “associate member” and “associated membership” have been removed, the German news agency dpa and the Reuters news agency reported on Thursday, adding that officials planned to make the statement public on Friday.

The reports come as the EU-Canada summit in Montreal, hosted by Canadian Prime Minister ⁠Mark Carney, is expected to start later on Thursday.

In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen raised the prospect of Canada becoming the 27-nation EU’s first “associate member” , a striking overture as both seek to pivot away from the United States under President Donald Trump.

However, Reuters and dpa report that von der Leyen’s suggestion of associate membership has been a divisive issue in negotiations among EU countries over ⁠the summit declaration, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several other leaders of fellow member nations pushing for the terms to be removed from the draft, citing diplomats.

The statement now calls for an “ever closer association” between Canada and the EU, and includes a joint initiative to improve international connectivity between Europe, Canada and Asia through “new ⁠subsea cable infrastructure”.

It also proposes conducting a joint feasibility study on Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and ⁠enabling young Canadians and Europeans to work across the Atlantic.

Deeper ties to Europe are an important part of Carney’s strategy to reduce Canada’s economic and security reliance on the US since Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. Still, Canada’s efforts to draw closer to the EU risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue.

Trump previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable” and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act”, the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.

Carney has aimed to deepen ties with the EU, Canada’s second-largest trading partner, since trade relations with the US, Ottawa’s largest economic partner, have been hampered under Trump.

The Canadian leader told reporters on Tuesday that the summit would be the launch of formal negotiations between the EU and Canada that would take another year.

“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”

Ferocious winds and torrential rain lashed India’s southeastern coast after a cyclone made landfall, killing at least three people before the storm weakened, officials said.

Cyclone Arnab hit southeastern Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday as a “very severe cyclonic storm”, with winds of 125-135km/h (77-84mph) and gusts reaching 150km/h in the early hours of Wednesday morning, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said.

About 50,000 people were told to move to safer areas in Andhra Pradesh and another 48,000 in neighbouring Odisha.

articles.title: Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, historic Mexican politician and former presidential candidate, dies at 92
articles.summary: Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate and one of Mexico’s most important modern political voices, died Wednesday at 92, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said.
articles.body: MEXICO CITY — Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate and one of Mexico’s most important modern political voices, died Wednesday at 92, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said. An undisputed leader of the Mexican left, Cárdenas was the son of one of the country’s most popular presidents — Gen. Lázaro Cárdenas. He was respected by allies and critics alike. Cárdenas played a pivotal role in Mexico’s democratization, beginning with his first presidential bid in 1988, which ended in a defeat widely regarded as the result of massive electoral fraud. He became Mexico City’s first popularly elected mayor in 1997. Cárdenas was so steadfast in his principles that in 2014 he resigned from the party he had founded in the late 1980s, the Democratic Revolution Party, because it governed the state of Guerrero when 43 students disappeared. Cárdenas also distanced himself from his longtime ally Andrés Manuel López Obrador when López Obrador became president in 2018. Cárdenas was “a man of firm principles,” Sheinbaum said on X, who transformed Mexico’s political life by leading “a peaceful democratic movement that channeled millions of Mexicans’ yearning for change.” “That historic election day, when he should have been recognized as president, marked the beginning of the democratic transformation. His dignity and republican convictions remain an essential reference point for our nation,” she added. Cárdenas, a civil engineer by training, was the son of President Lázaro Cárdenas, who nationalized the oil industry in 1938 and opened Mexico to refugees from the Spanish Civil War. The younger Cárdenas began his political career with the Institutional Revolutionary Party, better known as the PRI, and served as a senator and later as governor of the western state of Michoacán. In the late 1980s, he began leading a democratic faction within that party, from which he eventually broke away completely following electoral fraud. Together with other politicians, he founded the PRD in 1989 and ran as its presidential candidate in 1994 and 2000. Cárdenas ran for president again in 1994 and lost. In 1997, however, he became the first elected mayor of Mexico City, and in 2000 he once again ran for president and failed for a third time. The death was met by a swell of grief, including from former Mexican leaders across the political spectrum. Former Mexican President Vicente Fox wrote that “we were political adversaries but something bigger united us: the conviction that Mexico deserved complete democracy.” Sheinbaum’s predecessor and ally López Obrador called him a “pioneer of the democratic movement.” “Without him, the country’s political reality would be different. He was a transformative figure; he leaves us his teachings and ideals that never die,” López Obrador wrote on a post on X. He had three children with his wife, Celeste Batel, who has since passed away. One of them, Lázaro Cárdenas Batel, is also a politician.

articles.title: Michelle O'Neill says DUP has blocked her from PM meeting in Glasgow
articles.summary: The move follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests which prevented a contentious Orange Order march in Portadown.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has said Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly has "blocked" them from attending an economic summit involving Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The Sinn Féin vice-president and Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) minister were both invited to attend the National Economic Council in Glasgow on Friday alongside other devolved leaders.

The move follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests which prevented a contentious Orange Order march in Portadown from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road .

O'Neill described the move as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented".

"This is a reactive stunt, driven by the DUP's own internal pressures and electoral problems," she said in a statement posted online.

Little-Pengelly said the concerns arising from O'Neill's conduct and the "anger and hurt felt by many people across Northern Ireland, cannot simply be ignored or minimised".

She said the decision comes after stopping a separate planned engagement with the President of Ireland, Catherine Connolly.

"I have requested a separate meeting with the Prime Minister to ensure Northern Ireland's interests, including the urgent budgetary and funding challenges facing the Executive, continue to be represented directly," she added.

It emerges as a meeting of the DUP's ruling committee was due to take place on Thursday morning.

Party officers were expected to consider whether to withdraw the deputy first minister or cease official engagements with O'Neill, sources told the BBC's Nolan Live programme .

O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating last month's unnotified demonstrations in Portadown , with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

The Sinn Féin deputy leader has defended her involvement, saying it was the "right thing to do".

The prime minister revived the National Economic Council over the summer to encourage greater collaboration between the nations and regions.

In a statement posted online on Thursday , O'Neill said: "The deputy first minister has decided to block representation from here at a major political event, which would include meeting with the first ministers of Scotland and Wales, and the British prime minister.

"The Economic Forum is taking place tomorrow in Glasgow, and this reckless and irresponsible approach of Emma Little-Pengelly means the people of the north will not be represented.

"This is a reactive stunt, driven by the DUP's own internal pressures and electoral problems."

The DUP has been under pressure from unionist rivals and some within its own ranks over how to respond to the row over Drumcree.

Last week, DUP MP Carla Lockhart stepped down from the party's officer board over their leader Gavin Robinson not withdrawing Little-Pengelly to force O'Neill from their joint Stormont office.

Other DUP representatives including assembly member Diane Forsythe have since backed Lockhart's calls for O'Neill to be "removed from office" .

On Tuesday, Forsythe said that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".

On Wednesday, a second DUP assembly member called for O'Neill to go.

Maurice Bradley said removing O'Neill "would not, in itself, require the Assembly to collapse".

Bradley said the "attitude displayed by senior Sinn Féin representatives in the aftermath" of the dispute "have caused widespread anger and concern".

He said the "arrogance and defiance demonstrated by repeated declarations that Michelle O'Neill is 'going nowhere'" was "concerning".

Last week, a court heard Police Service of Northern Ireland intelligence information that dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on police had officers cleared a path for the parade.

Bradley's statement added: "No one is above the law, regardless of their political position. There cannot be one standard for ordinary citizens and another for those holding the highest offices in Northern Ireland."

Bradley added that the party "must stand together" and "support Carla Lockhart".

Other party members including former MP Lord McCrea and Mid Ulster councillor Clement Cuthbertson have also backed Lockhart.

Party leader Robinson said last week that he was "sorry" to see Lockhart quit the DUP's officer board but added that she remained "a key part of our team".

Speaking on the BBC's The View programme, the Robinson said the party had reached a democratic decision on how to deal with the Drumcree fallout.

He questioned whether it was necessary to "punish everyone in Northern Ireland when actually we should be punishing those who broke the law".

"We have considered all options and we keep all options on the table," he added.

articles.title: The San Francisco cottage linked to Gavin Newsom’s early childhood sold for $2.8 million in 2019; this month it went on the market for $4.5 million and sold in just 14 days for $5.85 million, more than double its price seven years ago
articles.summary: A home can gain value for many reasons, but a combination of location, land and an unusual family history can make it particularly attractive to buyers.
articles.body: A home can gain value for many reasons, but a combination of location, land and an unusual family history can make it particularly attractive to buyers. A redwood-clad cottage in San Francisco associated with California Governor Gavin Newsom’s early childhood has drawn attention after selling for $5.85 million, substantially above its asking price. According to The San Francisco Standard, which reported the sale on October 26, 2026, the two-bedroom property was listed for $4.5 million in early October and sold just 14 days later after attracting multiple all-cash offers. The sale price was more than double the $2.8 million it fetched in 2019, highlighting the appeal of the property’s location and development potential alongside its connection to Newsom’s family history.A quick sale above the asking priceThe property at 1284 Stanyan Street is located in the Cole Valley area of San Francisco, close to Mount Sutro Forest. The house measures less than 1,500 square feet and has two bedrooms and two bathrooms, but the surrounding land adds considerably to its appeal. The property comprises two adjoining parcels measuring nearly 10,000 square feet combined. One of the parcels opens onto Belgrave Avenue, while the wooded surroundings provide a degree of privacy that is unusual for a home within a major city.The property attracted multiple cash offers after entering the market in early October. It ultimately sold for $5.85 million, approximately $1.35 million above its asking price. The transaction closed 14 days after the listing, according to The San Francisco Standard. Listing agent John DiDomenico of Compass told The San Francisco Standard that the Newsom connection initially attracted attention, but the property's land value and potential were ultimately important factors behind the price.The home's connection to Gavin NewsomThe house has a history linked to Newsom’s maternal family. His maternal grandfather, Arthur Menzies, originally owned the property, which later passed to Newsom’s mother, Tessa Menzies. A 1967 election record listed Newsom’s father, William Newsom, as living at the Stanyan Street address around the time Gavin Newsom was born. However, the San Francisco Chronicle reported that although the records establish the family’s connection to the property, it is unclear exactly how long Newsom himself lived there as an infant.Newsom was born in San Francisco on October 10, 1967. His parents divorced in 1972, and his mother sold the property that year, according to public records cited by The San Francisco Standard. The home subsequently passed to another family, which reportedly owned it for more than four decades. The property’s historical association has added interest to its recent listing, although its location and land are also central to its real estate value.A small cottage on a sizeable plotBuilt in 1951, the house has undergone changes over the decades. Its exterior was clad in redwood sourced from Marin County in 1979. The kitchen and bathrooms have also been renovated, with work carried out in 2020 including updates to the kitchen, bathrooms and upstairs primary closet.The home features a deck, garden patios and views through the surrounding trees. It also includes a separate studio and a Japanese soaking tub. The two adjoining parcels offer room for potential expansion, subject to city approvals. The land may be particularly significant in a city where developable space is limited. The listing agent pointed to the property's location and future potential as important elements of its value, beyond the attention generated by the Newsom connection.From $2.8 million to $5.85 millionThe latest transaction marks a substantial increase from the property's 2019 sale price of $2.8 million. Its October 2026 sale price was $3.05 million higher, representing an increase of more than 100 per cent over seven years. The house had been listed for $3.6 million in May 2019 before selling for $2.8 million in July that year. The property also changed hands for $3.9 million in an off-market intra-family sale in 2025, according to The San Francisco Standard. Its latest sale followed a $4.5 million listing price and a swift round of offers.The transaction illustrates how a property’s value can reflect several factors at once: its location, the size and potential of its land, its condition and its history. In this case, the cottage’s connection to Newsom helped bring attention, while the land and its potential were identified by the listing agent as key considerations in the final price.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision?
