articles.title: Hello Kitty maker Sanrio cuts ties with TV spy show after China backlash
articles.summary: Hello Kitty maker Sanrio has canceled a collaboration with a Japanese TV spy show after a backlash in China, the second incident in days to highlight the tightrope foreign companies and celebrities must walk in the lucrative market.
articles.body: TOKYO — Hello Kitty maker Sanrio has canceled a collaboration with a Japanese TV spy show after a backlash in China, the second incident in days to highlight the tightrope foreign companies and celebrities must walk in the lucrative market. The Wednesday announcement by Sanrio’s Chinese subsidiary came just after French soccer star Kylian Mbappé apologized for remarks about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong that saw several Chinese sponsors cut ties with him. The hit show VIVANT, produced by Japanese broadcaster TBS and also available on Netflix, centers on Japanese spies and a terrorist organization called Tent. The latest season, currently being aired, depicts a fictional Chinese intelligence agency capturing and torturing some of the Japanese spies. Chinese anger over Sanrio’s range of soft toys, including Hello Kitty, dressed as spies from the show has simmered for days on social media and came to a head this week when Chinese state media ramped up the condemnation. “We deeply apologize for the concern this has caused everyone,” Sanrio’s Chinese subsidiary said in a statement. “Regarding this collaboration, we believe it contains expressions that are inconsistent with the corporate philosophy of the Sanrio Group. We have therefore decided to terminate this collaboration along with all subsequent projects and promotional activities.” TBS did not have immediate comment on the cancellation. TBS President Masamine Ryuho said at a regular news conference Wednesday that the drama is “entirely fictional and has no intention of disparaging any specific country,” local media reported. Relations between China and Japan have plunged since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said late last year that a hypothetical Chinese attack on the Beijing-claimed island of Taiwan could draw a military response from Tokyo.z China has urged its citizens not to travel to Japan and throttled exports of rare earths to the country, minerals vital to the manufacturing of everything from cars to weapons. Swaths of Japanese firms including Sanrio, however, are still reliant on the world’s second-biggest economy for sales. Sanrio booked sales of 9.8 billion yen ($62 million) in China in the first quarter, up almost 25% compared with the same period a year earlier. Foreign brands have often faced public backlash in China. ​Dolce & Gabbana canceled a Shanghai fashion show in 2018 after ads showed a Chinese woman struggling to eat pizza and spaghetti with chopsticks. ⁠In 2021, H&M, Nike and Adidas came under attack over comments made about labor conditions in Xinjiang.

articles.title: Spain train crash: Audio reveals chilling exchange between operators before deadly collision
articles.summary: Audio recordings released by Spanish media have shed light on the minutes before a train collision that killed at least 68 people and injured dozens,
articles.body: Audio recordings released by Spanish media have shed light on the minutes before a train collision that killed at least 68 people and injured dozens, raising questions about why a train was allowed to move while another remained stranded on the tracks.The recordings capture conversations between train drivers and a railway control centre in Madrid before the crash on Wednesday morning. Investigators are examining the circumstances in which a train travelling from Madrid to Seville struck another train that had stopped ahead of it.The disaster has triggered three days of national mourning in Spain and renewed concerns about railway safety, with officials investigating a possible signalling failure and the decisions taken by railway controllers.According to the recordings published by Spanish outlets including El País and RTVE, a technical problem had disrupted the automatic signalling system, forcing trains on the affected stretch to stop. The system helps control train movements and prevents trains from entering sections of track when it may be unsafe to do so.Spain's transport minister said the Renfe train was later instructed to move again in "error", without speed restrictions.Recordings capture exchanges One recording captures a control centre operator telling the driver of the Renfe train to continue at normal speed after technical problems."Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation," the control centre operator says to the driver.The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."Lateral Signalling Block is an alternative procedure used when the regular automatic signalling or data transmission system fails. It allows train movements to continue under a different operating arrangement.In another recording, the driver of the Iryo train reports losing communication with the train control system and says the train is stationary at Urda.The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator.Following several exchanges, the driver is instructed to "resume the journey" normally.However, a later recording appears to show that the Iryo train was still unable to move. Its driver contacts the control centre again and explains that a problem with the train's security system is preventing it from restarting."The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.The exchange suggests that the control centre had been informed that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached. Investigators will need to establish how the two trains were managed and whether the procedures followed were appropriate.Officials question decision The Renfe train was carrying 397 passengers, while the Iryo train had 147 people on board. Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by the Renfe service.Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente described the decision to allow trains to move again without speed restrictions as "inexplicable". The investigation is expected to examine the signalling disruption, communications between drivers and controllers, and the instructions issued before the collision.Emergency workers spent the night at the crash site using powerful floodlights to search damaged carriages and recover victims. Some bodies remained unidentified as recovery operations continued.Spain's interior ministry said hundreds of personnel had been deployed to help at the site. Drones and helicopters were also being used to locate victims and clear rubble.Witnesses described scenes of devastation, with passengers trapped in their seats, people crying and bleeding, and smoke filling the carriages. One carriage caught fire.Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said the "whole of Spain is grieving", adding that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense".Sánchez also said it was "unacceptable" that Spain had experienced two serious rail disasters this year. A separate high-speed train crash near Córdoba in January killed 46 people on the same line, although at a location much further south.Crash sparks protests The disaster has prompted political reactions and public anger over railway safety. Most political parties suspended campaigning for upcoming elections following the crash.The far-right Vox party was an exception. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of Spain's rail infrastructure.Around 1,500 people gathered outside the Spanish Transport Ministry in Madrid overnight, broadcaster TVE reported. Many demonstrators called for the resignations of Sánchez and Puente.Police used tear gas to disperse the crowd after protesters threw bottles and flares. No injuries or arrests were reported.Railway drivers are also expected to proceed with a planned strike on Thursday. The Spanish Union of Railway Drivers, known as Semaf, said the action would be held "in defence of railway safety".Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of Spain's main opposition People's Party, said "Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure."The recordings have raised questions about the decisions made in the minutes before the collision, but they do not by themselves establish the cause of the crash. Investigators will have to determine how the signalling failure occurred, why the trains were instructed to move and whether any safety rules were breached.You use AI every day. articles.summary: An Applebee's customer noticed the payment kiosk suggested an $11.30 tip on a $49.49 bill, sparking questions about after-tax tipping practices. Experts stress the importance of transparency.
articles.body: A customer is raising questions about tipping practices at Applebee's after noticing that the suggested gratuity on his bill was higher than he expected. The customer, who shared his experience in a TikTok video, questioned why the restaurant's payment kiosk suggested an $11.30 tip on a $49.49 bill. A 20% tip on $49.49 would amount to $9.90 — about $1.40 less than the suggested amount. SHAKE SHACK CUSTOMER HITS 'NO TIP' AT KIOSK, THEN WATCHES PRICES JUMP IN VIRAL VIDEO The apparent explanation was that the kiosk calculated the suggested gratuity on the after-tax total of $56.50, rather than the $49.49 subtotal. The payment screen indicated that tips were calculated after tax and before discounts, according to the video. Fox News Digital reached out to Applebee's and the customer for comment. Robert Mahon, managing partner of New York City-based Mahon Hospitality Group, told Fox News Digital that restaurants generally have some control over how their payment systems calculate suggested gratuities. AUTOMATIC TIP OR SERVICE CHARGE? NEW STATE LAW REQUIRES RESTAURANTS TO TELL DINERS BEFORE THEY ORDER "It varies from restaurant to restaurant," he said. "The systems come with default settings, but the restaurant can usually change them. We use Toast, which defaults to calculating tips before tax, and there's a setting in the back office to switch it." "You're tipping for the food, drinks and service — adding tax into that calculation doesn't really make sense to me," he said. "Guests can always leave more if they want." articles.title: Ted Bundy could have more undiscovered victims after DNA links him to murder of chief's daughter: detective
articles.summary: DNA evidence linked Ted Bundy to Melissa Ann Smith's 1974 murder, but a cold-case detective says the serial killer may have unknown victims.
articles.body: A DNA breakthrough has solved the 52-year-old murder of a Utah police chief's teenage daughter, and the cold-case detective who helped crack it says notorious serial killer Ted Bundy could have other victims investigators do not even know about. Melissa Ann Smith, 17, the daughter of then-Midvale Police Chief Louis Smith, was found dead in 1974. For decades, investigators suspected Bundy but lacked the evidence needed to definitively tie him to her murder. That changed in July, when DNA evidence in the killing of another 17-year-old Utah girl, Laura Ann Aime, was matched to Bundy, allowing investigators to compare evidence preserved from Smith's case for more than half a century. POTENTIAL MICHIGAN SERIAL KILLER MAY HAVE LEFT BEHIND VALUABLE EVIDENCE, FORMER FBI PROFILER SAYS "There may be more victims out there that we're not even aware of, and I think there's always been that speculation," Salt Lake County Sheriff's Office Detective Ben Pender told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview Wednesday. Pender, a 35-year law enforcement veteran assigned to the Salt Lake County Sheriff's Office unsolved homicide and missing person unit, said investigators plan to preserve the evidence that helped solve Smith's murder so it can potentially be used in other cases. FORMER CHICAGO POLICE DETECTIVE LINKED BY DNA TO 8-YEAR-OLD GIRL'S COLD-CASE MURDER, POLICE SAY "We're gonna hold on to this evidence, and we're gonna utilize it in cases that we believe may be connected to see if we can't resolve not only our case, but anybody else who may have a case with Bundy," Pender said. Smith's body was discovered by hunters on Oct. 27, 1974, in a wooded area near the border of Summit and Salt Lake counties. COLD CASE BREAKTHROUGH SOLVES TEEN KILLING AFTER SUSPECT LIVED FREE FOR DECADES: 'BETTER BE AFRAID' "These cases that are unsolved are unsolved, in my opinion, for a reason, and because they are extremely difficult to solve," Pender said. Although investigators had long suspected Bundy, similarities between Smith's killing and his other crimes were not enough to definitively tie him to her death. FORENSIC GENEALOGY UNMASKS COLD CASE SUSPECT AS STRANGLER, SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES LATER: OFFICIALS Investigators needed evidence establishing that Bundy was responsible rather than relying on a similar method of operation, Pender said. "DNA is not always the answer, but it definitely is a piece that's missing a lot of times in these cases that, with everything else with the case, will maybe bring that together," Pender said. COVERT DNA SAMPLE FROM COLORADO MAN'S TRASH REVIVES 44-YEAR-OLD TEXAS MURDER CASE: REPORT The break investigators needed ultimately came from the Aime case. Aime vanished after leaving a Halloween party to buy cigarettes on Oct. 31, 1974. Her body was discovered by hikers near American Fork Canyon days later, and investigators determined she had been raped, strangled and murdered. DETECTIVE SUSPECTED IN GIRL’S MURDER MAY HAVE KILLED OTHERS, FORMER INVESTIGATOR FEARS Bundy was considered the prime suspect for decades, but authorities lacked evidence conclusively tying him to the killing. Investigators eventually developed a DNA profile from evidence in Aime's case that was linked to Bundy. Remaining evidence from her case then gave investigators an opportunity to compare it with evidence preserved from Smith's killing. NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS Pender said investigators had retained reports and evidence from the original Smith investigation, including evidence collected during her postmortem examination. Utah County investigators reached out to Summit County after the breakthrough in the Aime case to determine whether the remaining evidence could help resolve Smith's murder. Summit County then turned to Pender because Salt Lake County had maintained evidence from the 1974 investigation. Investigators worked with the Utah Bureau of Forensic Services to compare DNA evidence from the two cases and determined the profiles matched. The DNA findings, combined with evidence involving Bundy's pattern, motive, means and opportunity, led authorities to conclude Bundy killed Smith and formally close her case Tuesday, 52 years to the day after her body was found. The breakthrough would not have been possible without evidence preserved by investigators for more than five decades. "It's extremely important, in all of these cases, to preserve the evidence," Pender said. "We, in all homicide cases, we maintain that evidence forever." "We don't ever get rid of that, even if a case is resolved or solved, and we don't get rid of it for this very reason," he added. But Pender cautioned that solving one decades-old murder through DNA does not mean investigators can simply run every unsolved killing potentially connected to Bundy through a database. Each case is different. Some have DNA evidence while others do not, and evidence collected decades ago may have degraded, been handled before investigators understood the importance of preserving DNA or contain genetic material from multiple people. "Back then, DNA wasn't a thing, so nobody knew of it," Pender said. Advances in forensic technology continue to give investigators new opportunities to examine old evidence, but the limitations of individual cases remain. Pender said his caseload includes 34 unsolved homicides and 14 adult missing person cases in which investigators suspect foul play. He stressed that those cases are not believed to be connected to Bundy, with one notable exception. Nancy Wilcox remains missing, and Pender said Bundy confessed to killing her. Her body has never been recovered, preventing investigators from closing the case based solely on his confession. Smith's case, Pender said Tuesday, "does not close the book on Ted Bundy." Investigators intend to continue working on Wilcox's disappearance and preserve the Bundy evidence for any other cases in which it could prove useful. Other cases potentially tied to Bundy could also yield new answers through DNA, Pender said. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "I think it's definitely possible," Pender said. "It just depends on what information other agencies maybe have in their particular cases." Pender emphasized that cooperation among law enforcement agencies was critical to solving Smith's murder, with Summit, Salt Lake and Utah counties working alongside the state crime lab. "It's more about the victim, right? It's about the victim, the family, the community, it's about resolving the case," Pender said. "It's still important that we connect them the right way, and we don't just … throw everything on to Ted Bundy that we're not quite sure of." articles.title: ‘Mobilized whole-of-government response to that joke’: Obama mocks Trump over Cheesecake Factory jibe
articles.summary: Former US president Barack Obama has slammed President Donald Trump and the Republican Party for focusing on his joke about the White House makeover
articles.body: Former US president Barack Obama has slammed President Donald Trump and the Republican Party for focusing on his joke about the White House makeover instead of addressing inflation, accusing the administration of mobilising the entire government to respond to his remarks.“They mobilized a whole-of-government response to that joke, not to inflation, but to that joke,” Obama said at a campaign rally in suburban Atlanta, Georgia, on Wednesday, in the final week of the US midterm election campaign.“This is what I mean when I say these are not serious people. They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory,” he added.Obama was referring to his recent remarks comparing Trump's gold-heavy White House renovations to Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein opening a Cheesecake Factory. The former president had made the joke during a campaign stop in Cleveland, Ohio, last week, drawing a sharp response from Trump.Trump, who has been travelling across the country to campaign for Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, hit back at Obama, calling him a “lousy president” and defending the restaurant chain as a “very successful company”.At Wednesday's rally, Obama said he had heard that Trump was unhappy with his remarks but argued that the administration's response had missed the bigger issue of rising prices facing American voters.“The guy who is trying to figure out how to lower inflation ... they told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said, referring to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had mocked his comments outside a branch of the restaurant in Washington.Obama also defended his reference to the popular restaurant chain, saying he had frequently visited it while raising his two daughters.“I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?” he said, adding that Chuck E. Cheese and California Pizza Kitchen had also been regular family destinations.Turning to the cost-of-living crisis, Obama said the administration should be more concerned about the rising cost of eating out and other expenses affecting Americans.The former president also recalled the controversy over a tan suit he wore during his presidency, saying, “I am old enough to remember when a president wearing a tan suit was a major national controversy.”Obama was in Georgia to campaign for Democratic senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election, and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, along with other Democratic candidates.Ossoff also attacked Trump during the rally, accusing him of leading a corrupt administration and warning that Democrats would hold the president accountable if they regained control of Congress.Bottoms, meanwhile, sought to draw a contrast with her Republican opponent, billionaire healthcare executive Rick Jackson, accusing him of putting wealthy interests ahead of taxpayers.The rally came as both Obama and Trump intensified their campaign appearances ahead of the midterm elections, with control of Congress and several key state races at stake.You use AI every day. articles.title: Brother dies in a road accident in 2019, leaving his unmarried sister dependent on him; insurer refuses Rs 5 lakh death benefit because sisters are not listed, but Allahabad HC orders payment to her as legal heir
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Allahabad high court has ruled that an unmarried sister cannot be denied the accidental death benefit merely because she is not listed as a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Allahabad high court has ruled that an unmarried sister cannot be denied the accidental death benefit merely because she is not listed as a covered family member. It directed an insurance company to pay Rs 5 lakh to a woman whose claim it had rejected.In its October 26, 2026, order, the high court quashed the Oriental Insurance Company’s rejection of the claim under the Mukhyamantri Kisan Evam Sarvahit Bima Yojana.Why did the insurance company reject the claim?As per the court order, the woman’s brother died in a road accident on May 18, 2019. She said that he was the sole breadwinner of the household and that she, being unmarried, was dependent on him.After his death, she sought Rs 5 lakh under the state’s insurance scheme. In October 2019, the insurance company rejected her claim, saying that a sister was not included in the definition of family in the scheme’s memorandum of understanding.The matter was then placed before the district committee in Basti. After considering a report from the sub-divisional magistrate, the committee recorded that the deceased was the head of the family and directed the insurer to accept the claim and make the payment.The woman was informed of this decision in March 2021. The company, however, maintained its rejection, reiterating that a sister was not eligible for the benefit after her brother’s death.The woman then approached the high court. She argued that she was her brother’s legal heir and that the scheme provided for payment to a nominee or legal heir after the accidental death of the insured head or breadwinner of a family.The insurer countered that its liability was governed by the memorandum of understanding and the policy, and that a sister was not among the family members covered under them.Why did the high court rule in her favour?A division bench of Justice Garima Prashad and Justice Prakash Padia examined the distinction between people covered for insurance benefits and those entitled to receive the money after the insured person’s death.The bench noted that the scheme covered the head or breadwinner for personal accident insurance of up to Rs 5 lakh. A separate provision stated that, in the event of the insured person’s accidental death during the policy period, the amount had to be paid to the nominee or legal heir.“The omission of a sister from the list of covered family members cannot itself create such a dispute or defeat the express provision for payment to a legal heir,” the court noted.The bench also noted that the insurer had wrongly applied the clause defining covered family members to decide who could receive the death benefit. It said the agreement did not restrict payment to a legal heir who was also a covered family member.The court then clarified that this did not mean sisters were automatically covered for their own accidental injuries or medical treatment under the scheme. The ruling concerned only entitlement to receive the death benefit after the insured breadwinner’s death.The high court allowed the woman’s petition and quashed the rejection communicated by Oriental Insurance Company on April 16, 2021.It directed the insurer to pay Rs 5 lakh within four weeks from the date the company receives a certified copy of the judgment. The district magistrate, Basti, was directed to facilitate payment under the claim procedure.The court made no order on costs.

articles.title: Russia strikes Dnipro train station in central Ukraine, killing 14
articles.summary: A Russian drone struck the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro as people waited to board a train on Thursday morning, killing 14 people.
articles.body: A Russian drone struck the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro as people waited to board a train on Thursday morning, killing 14 people. Another 10 people were wounded in the strike, the latest in a series of Russian attacks targeting civilian spaces as well as transport and energy infrastructure in Ukraine. At least 19 people including two 15-year-old girls were killed across the country on Thursday, authorities said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the Dnipro strike as “horrific” and called for more sanctions to deter further Russian attacks. “Just how many terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and the Russian energy sector, rather than de-escalating?” Zelensky wrote in a social media post. Offering condolences to bereaved families, Zelensky said sanctions “against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues.” US President Donald Trump waived a slate of sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales earlier this month, angering Kyiv, which has long advocated for tougher sanctions on Russian energy exports. Russian state media reported on Wednesday that Washington was in talks with the Kremlin to lift sanctions on Russia’s multibillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund almost five years after they were put in place by the Biden administration following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Zelensky said there were two trains at the station in Dnipro when the drone struck. Footage from the scene shows several bodies strewn across the platform. The head of the hospital where the wounded were taken told local media many of the injured had suffered shrapnel wounds, and four people were having emergency surgery. Thursday’s victims included two 15-year-old girls killed in a Russian strike on the northern city of Chernihiv. Another three people were killed by a Russian drone strike on a residential building in the Poltava region. Elsewhere, in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, Russia and Ukraine have since Tuesday been observing a ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump. Fighting has paused in the area to allow for the evacuation of the elderly and the vulnerable from Oleshky, where thousands have been trapped by fighting without electricity or fresh food and water supplies. The temporary halt in strikes will also allow critically needed supplies to come in. Both sides have adhered to the ceasefire conditions, which will remain in place until 10:59 p.m. local time on November 1.

articles.title: Richard Simmons lived in this Hollywood Hills home from the 1980s until his death in 2024; the estate has sold for $3.8 million after initially asking $6.99 million; new owner plans to restore its classic roots
articles.summary: The Sunset Strip estate in Los Angeles, where fitness guru Richard Simmons lived for decades, has sold for $3.827 million, a TMZ report confirmed.
articles.body: The Sunset Strip estate in Los Angeles, where fitness guru Richard Simmons lived for decades, has sold for $3.827 million, a TMZ report confirmed. The Hollywood Hills estate, which features a Colonial-style home, initially asked $6.99 million. The new owner plans to restore the home, listing agents Rachelle Rosten and Kelly deLaat of Douglas Elliman told the outlet. The buyer has not been publicly identified.The property first went on the market in June 2025 with an asking price of $6.99 million, Realtor.com reported. This was about a year after Simmons died. The house drew interest; however, none of it resulted in a deal. An earlier sale went into escrow at $5.889 million but fell apart in December. The seller cut the price to $5.799 million, and another buyer signed a contract in May. The final price came in nearly $2 million below that reduced asking price.A home with a famous pedigreeThe fitness guru owned the home for decades. Simmons bought it in the 1980s and stayed for more than four decades. He preferred to maintain his privacy in his final years and loved spending time in the Colonial-style home. Simmons died in July 2024, just days after his 76th birthday.Like many other prospective buyers, the new owner was attracted by the home's pedigree. While the identity of the new owner remains under wraps, TMZ confirmed that he “isn’t anyone famous”. The buyer has plans for the home, including restoring its classic roots. “The perfect buyer found this home. Drawn to its rich history, heritage, and pedigree, he plans to restore it to its classic roots,” Rosten told the tabloid. Paul Czako of Gussman Czako Estates represented the buyer.Inside the Colonial-style homeThe hilltop home sits on a gated parcel of 0.56 acres above the Sunset Strip, one of Los Angeles’ most prestigious residential areas. The listing agent, Rachelle Rosten, said the value lay in the land. “The true value lies in the land itself,” she told the outlet. The agents said their asking price accounted for the cost of renovation, construction and permits, as many comparable homes nearby would require major work.The existing house has four bedrooms and roughly 5,000 square feet of space, with panoramic city views. The buyer also gets the house’s personal details, including cherubs on the staircase, patterned wallpaper, curved French doors and an attic gym. The house was originally built in 1937, according to the listing on Douglas Elliman. The listing says the property offers “a rare development opportunity in one of Los Angeles’ most coveted and recognisable locations”.Described as an “ideal canvas for a world-class estate”, the property offers ample space to expand the existing home or build a larger, modern mansion from scratch.“The grounds feature multiple usable tiers, including generous flat pads, terraced gardens, and a pool level, providing flexibility for new construction, guest structures, or a reimagined compound. With its premier positioning just moments from Sunset Plaza and its exceptional views, this is a chance to build or transform a showpiece residence in a setting defined by prestige, privacy, and sweeping outlooks,” the listing says.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Rescue teams search wreckage for survivors after train crash in Spain
articles.summary: A canine unit and cranes have been deployed to aid search and rescue efforts following the deadly crash.
articles.body:
Rescuers in Spain are searching for victims and survivors a day after a train struck another from behind, killing 68 people , in the country’s second high-speed rail disaster this year.

Emergency workers and rescue teams with sniffer dogs continued to look for victims on Thursday morning, a day after the collision in Toledo province, central Spain.

Cranes were in place to help shift the carriages as police and soldiers helped to pick through the wreckage strewn down the gravel slope where at least three train carriages were derailed by the impact.

Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, told TVE that teams were working “very carefully, because we still cannot say with certainty that there are no more victims trapped in the twisted wreckage”.

“A canine unit was deployed yesterday. They will go back in today to make sure that nobody else remains there,” she added.

She said 53 people remained in hospital, with 15 in critical care.

Three days of mourning have been declared for those killed in the accident.

Wednesday’s crash followed a similar fatal accident earlier this year involving the same rail companies on the same line.

In January, 46 people died when a train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going in the opposite way in southern Spain.

The collision has reopened a national debate about the safety of Spain’s high-speed rail network, the biggest in Europe and, until recently, a source of national pride.

Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the crash happened after several trains stopped automatically due to a signal failure.

A state-run Renfe train was then authorised to proceed at normal speed even though a stationary Iryo-operated train was ahead.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited the crash site on Wednesday. He pledged an investigation into the latest collision and promised improvements to prevent another tragedy like the two that have shaken trust in a rail system that carried 45 million travellers last year, including millions of tourists.

“It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail,” Sanchez said. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.”

The Spanish train drivers’ union, SEMAF, said that it does not want to speculate on the cause of the crash.

“We wish to exercise caution until we have a detailed understanding of exactly what happened, so as not to engage in speculation,” SEMAF said in a statement late on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, SEMAF said train drivers have gone ahead with a previously planned strike to push for more railway safety and structural change.

articles.title: Protests erupt in Spain after train crash kills dozens
articles.summary: Protests erupted in Madrid as Spain began mourning the 68 people killed and dozens injured in the country’s deadliest train crash in decades.
articles.body: URDA, Spain — Spain began three days of mourning Thursday after at least 69 people were killed and dozens more injured in the country’s deadliest train crash in decades. But anger is mounting about the alleged incompetence that allowed the accident to happen and protesters clashed with police overnight outside the country’s transport ministry. Once considered one of the country’s crowning achievements, Spain’s high-speed rail network had not endured a deadly crash since it came into service over 30 years ago. After the second train accident in less than a year, the tragedy has deepened the feeling among many that there is something broken in Spanish society. The crash follows weeks of protests. Rising costs and a housing shortage that is pricing many Spaniards out of the housing market, have already triggered massive and sometimes deadly protests across the country, and piled the pressure on the Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. On Wednesday, four weeks before the country goes to the polls in a national election, Sanchez visited the site in the central province of Toledo where a quiet stretch of rail lined by olive groves had been turned into a scene of devastation. Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off. Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident in the countryside in the province of Toledo after one train crashed into another that was stationary on the line. Hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police, firefighters and soldiers attended the scene to rescue survivors and recover bodies, before cranes were brought in to move parts of the damaged trains late Wednesday. Several Americans were hurt, according to the State Department, which did not provide further details. Jacksonville firefighter Josue Garcia-Otero was on board with seven of his family members. “We got to safety first, then began treating other patients that were critically injured,” Garcia-Otero said in a news release issued by the Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department. “My wife is a nurse, and she was helping too.” Pledging an investigation and improvements to prevent a similar tragedy in future, Sánchez said it was clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail.” It was “not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year,” he said, referring to an incident in January when 46 people died after one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in the south of the country. Both crashes involved trains operated by the state-owned RENFE company and the privately owned IRYO. His transport minister, Óscar Puente, said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. Puente, who is facing calls to resign, said the train engineers were not to blame, but instead a security system had stopped working because of a computer malfunction, causing all trains on the line to stop at about 8:30 a.m. local time (5:30 a.m. ET). Shortly afterwards he said central command had told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, adding that never should have happened and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m. Riot police used tear gas outside his transport ministry in Madrid late Wednesday after far-right protesters gathered outside and pushed against a cordon set up by officers. Some threw flares and other objects as some chanted slogans against Puente and Sánchez. Quite what effect the accident will have on Sánchez’s political ambitions remains unclear. The prime minister called a snap election next month after his Socialist party suffered several defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country’s housing crisis. His minority government had put forward two decree laws aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market after nationwide protests following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid apartment. Maricarmen Abascal, who was a wheelchair user, was eventually allowed to return but died in hospital before she could do so. Sánchez who took power in 2018 has weathered several crises during his premiership including the Covid-19 pandemic and the global inflation rise. But he has faced attacks from right-wing parties over his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both deny, and polls show he is facing and uphill battle to win votes ahead of the election next month.

articles.title: Protest at India university where no students’ union vote held for 20 years
articles.summary: Jamia Millia Islamia campus in Indian capital has seen weeks of protests, with several students holding a hunger strike.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – Today is the 18th day of an indefinite hunger strike for Ebin Basil, a third-year student of law at Jamia Millia Islamia, a prominent Muslim university on the southeastern edge of the Indian capital.

Basil, 23, has been fasting since October 12 for the restoration of the university’s students’ union, which has been suspended for the past 20 years.

Surrounded by dozens of friends and supporters, he remains resolute as his frail body lies on a mat inside the university’s political science department building. “Till my last breath, I will be fighting,” he told Al Jazeera.

Basil is among five hunger strikers at the core of the protest, which has seen hundreds of Jamia students congregating in the grounds surrounding a statue of iconic Urdu-Persian poet Mirza Ghalib, near the university’s main entrance. Several other students who initially joined the hunger strike have withdrawn over health concerns.

The protest began this month with students holding night vigils and calling for the students’ union election. On October 16, the university suspended Basil for a year and banned two other hunger strikers from the campus. By the night of October 17, nearly 200 protesters had returned to the grounds, and their demonstrations continued.

On October 24, the entrance gates to the university were barricaded, classes moved online, and students in halls of residence were pressured to leave. Armed police and paramilitary forces were stationed outside the gate, and a ban on gatherings of more than four people was imposed on campus.

On Monday, the university administration announced that elections would be held within 15 days of the approval of a draft union constitution to be prepared according to the guidelines of the University Grants Commission, the body that controls India’s state universities.

Jamia has set a December 20 deadline for a committee to draft the union constitution and to hold elections within 15 days of the draft’s approval. But no deadline for approval has been set, prompting the students to reject the university’s offer as “too slow”.

“It is a very vague point,” Basil told Al Jazeera.

Jamia Millia Islamia’s relationship with student democracy has been marked by long interruptions.

Established in 1920 – Thursday is its 106th anniversary – Jamia was granted federal university status in 1988 and had its minority status formally recognised by the National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions in 2011.

The first student union election at Jamia was held in 1981. Elections were discontinued in 1997 amid campus unrest and resumed in 2005. But that union was dissolved the following year, with the university administration blaming an alleged attack on the vice-chancellor.

Since then, several attempts have been made to revive the union, including a high court petition in 2011 and a student hunger strike in 2017. Meanwhile, to ease the pressure, the university allowed elected department-level student bodies that did not have influence over the whole campus.

As the current protest drags on, Basil’s health continues to deteriorate. He has lost 7kg and can barely walk unaided. Blood tests show his sodium and glucose levels are low.

“My condition is very bad. I am not even able to walk on my own right now,” he said, adding that his mental health was also suffering.

Around him, the campus has turned into a fortress, with hundreds of police and paramilitary personnel guarding its gates. Classes and exams have been moved online and the university has been closed until January 13, with students in university accommodation asked to vacate their rooms.

“They have closed the university gates completely and built a wall in front of them,” Basil said.

Jamia students say an elected union would give them a collective voice to raise concerns over conditions in halls of residence, canteens, fee increases, and restrictions imposed by the university administration on joining the youth-led antigovernment protests being held across the country.

“If a union comes, the students will have power, and the administration will not have the arbitrary power it has now,” Basil said.

M K Nausheen Farook, a second-year master’s student in disaster management, agrees.

“We are continuing this protest because we have not got a proper election date. We do not trust the Jamia administration,” said the 23-year-old student from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, accusing the authorities of acting at the behest of the federal government controlled by the right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which is known for its anti-Muslim policies.

Farook also alleged that women residents in university accommodation were being pressured to leave after classes went online.

Mantasha Irfan, a master’s student of peace and conflict studies and member of the left-wing All India Students’ Association (AISA), said the protesters are facing immediate difficulties due to the administration’s crackdown.

“They have cut off our basic supplies. There is just one functioning toilet for hundreds of student protesters. There is no water or electricity,” she told Al Jazeera. “Even women students who are menstruating do not have access to sanitary pads, and they are not allowing people to bring them in.”

Irfan, 23, said the demand for a union must also be understood through Jamia’s history of political mobilisation around issues affecting the Muslim community.

“Whenever something has happened to Muslims, Jamia and AMU have been at the forefront of the struggle and important centres of resistance,” she said.

AMU refers to Aligarh Muslim University, India’s largest minority institution, located about 120km (74 miles) away in Uttar Pradesh state.

‘To discourage emergence of Muslim leaders’

After weeks of similar protests, which included a 19-day hunger strike by a number of students, authorities at AMU announced this month that students’ union elections would be held on November 5.

The AMU election would come eight years after the last students’ union was formed there, forcing many to question why Muslim institutions continue to be denied a representative body, while other prominent universities known for student activism, such as Jawaharlal Nehru University and Delhi University, continue to elect student bodies every year.

Apoorvanand, professor of Hindi at Delhi University, who goes by a single name, told Al Jazeera that Jamia and AMU occupy a distinct position because of their Muslim minority character.

“The government and university administrations are unwilling to encourage independent thinking among Muslim students or the emergence of Muslim leaders,” he said.

Apoorvanand said students across India are feeling increasingly suffocated by the “erosion of democratic spaces” on the campuses. “They are now prepared to go to any extent to ensure that democratic spaces are restored, including at Jamia Millia Islamia,” he said.

Jamia authorities say they are trying to end the standoff.

Spokeswoman Saima Saeed told Al Jazeera that their administration is “the first in 20 years” to accept the students’ demand for a union. She said the proposed constitution requires careful examination of court orders, government recommendations and the university’s statutes, adding that Jamia’s “bona fide students and employees are its primary and genuine stakeholders”.

Meanwhile, many students find themselves caught in the ongoing standoff, as they hope to return to in-person classes.

Hera Sarfaraz, a first-year master’s student in business administration, told Al Jazeera that ordinary students are suffering. They want the university administration and the protesters to resolve the issue amicably and allow academic life to resume.

“We want our regular classes back and do not want to miss out on in-person learning by being confined to online classes. This limits our exposure to university life,” she said.

articles.title: Pentagon probes possible cyberattack after freezer failures spoil food at US bases
articles.summary: US military investigators are examining whether hackers deliberately tampered with refrigeration systems at military bases across America after a series
articles.body: US military investigators are examining whether hackers deliberately tampered with refrigeration systems at military bases across America after a series of freezer malfunctions spoiled food in August, according to four officials familiar with the matter.The Pentagon is also in contact with French counterparts investigating a similar incident that disrupted commercial freezers at supermarkets in France earlier this month, one of the officials said.Reuters could not establish how far the US investigation had progressed or whether investigators had identified the cause of the malfunctions or those responsible.The Pentagon said a unit of US Cyber Command, the military's cyber force, was "working in close coordination with interagency and law enforcement partners". It did not provide further details.The US Army Criminal Investigation Division confirmed that its Cyber Field Office was involved and was working with French law enforcement to better understand "the refrigeration outages in Europe".The suspected attack affected at least six military commissaries, which are on-base shops where service personnel buy food, according to a Reuters review of social media posts and website updates published by the affected bases in August.Freezers allegedly switched to heating modeThe incidents occurred in late August and involved more than ordinary equipment failures. In at least one case, the temperature settings of refrigeration units were raised overnight, leaving large quantities of food spoiled by the following morning.A Facebook post from Fort Huachuca in Arizona on August 26 described what had happened to its freezer.The account said the unit "went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food. Trust us when we say it was 'spoiled.'"The possibility that the incidents involved deliberate cyber interference was first reported on August 28 by the recently launched blog Signal and Silence.The involvement of military investigators and their contacts with French authorities were subsequently reported by Stars and Stripes and Britain's Daily Telegraph. Reuters is now reporting for the first time that the Pentagon is treating the incidents as a suspected hack.French supermarket attack offers possible cluesThe US investigation comes after a similar incident in France, where hackers reportedly altered temperature controls on commercial refrigeration units at more than 350 establishments.Supermarkets were forced to remove spoiled frozen food from their shelves. In some cases, temperatures were raised so sharply that refrigeration units caught fire. One supermarket owner estimated earlier this month that the damage nationwide could run into tens of millions of euros.Experts previously told Reuters that the French attack appeared relatively easy to carry out. Danish refrigeration technology company Danfoss said many of the controllers used in the affected units were obsolete or running outdated firmware, potentially making them easier to compromise.Reuters could not determine whether Danfoss equipment, or controllers made by another manufacturer, were installed at the affected US military bases. Danfoss did not respond to requests for comment.Why refrigeration systems are a cybersecurity riskRefrigeration is essential to keeping food safe during storage and distribution. If hackers can remotely change a cooling system's settings, they may be able to spoil food without shutting the equipment down entirely.The Global Food Safety Initiative, an industry body, earlier this year urged food safety professionals and information technology leaders to work together to ensure "robust cybersecurity" for refrigeration systems. It warned that "a hacked cooling system is just as dangerous as a broken one."Previous incidents have demonstrated the risks. Danfoss said hackers targeted or accessed supermarkets in Russia and Israel in 2022 that were using outdated versions of its refrigeration controllers.In December last year, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles accused a Ukrainian woman of belonging to a hacking group that disrupted refrigeration at a meatpacking facility in 2024, ruining more than 2,000 pounds of meat.Bill Moore, chief executive of industrial cybersecurity firm Xona Systems, said refrigeration controllers were originally designed to be managed by technicians working on site. Increasingly, however, such equipment is connected to the internet, potentially exposing it to remote attacks.The risks extend beyond refrigeration, but the consequences can be particularly serious when food storage is involved. "It can definitely disrupt the supply chain for food," Moore said.Investigators have yet to establish whether the US military incidents were caused by hackers, how the systems may have been accessed or who could have been responsible. If a cyberattack is confirmed, the case would highlight how digital interference with seemingly ordinary equipment can threaten food supplies and critical infrastructure.You use AI every day. articles.title: South West Water given lowest environmental rating
articles.summary: The water firm is performing "significantly below target" for pollution, the Environment Agency says.
articles.body:
South West Water has been given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency over high levels of pollution.

The regulator downgraded the firm from two stars out of a possible four to one, meaning it is now considered a "poor performing company" for its environmental impact.

It said it had performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents for the 15th year in a row.

South West Water, which has 1.8 million customers across Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of Dorset and Somerset, said it knew there was "much more to do" and was taking action to improve areas that "matter most" to customers and the environment.

The annual Environmental Performance Assessment grades England's nine water and sewerage companies largely on how often they pollute rivers, streams and the sea.

For 2025, South West Water was among four companies rated as poor performing, or one star, while four others were rated as requiring improvement, two stars.

Severn Trent Water was the only company to achieve the highest rating of four stars.

The Environment Agency's report card comes a month after South West Water was fined almost £8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years.

In the last year it also recorded the sharpest rise in customer complaints of any water company .

Serious incidents in the past year include pollution in St Austell River , killing thousands of fish, while pollution at Exmouth meant beachgoers had to leave the water .

Industry regulator Ofwat said the company met seven of its 23 targets in 2025-26, with below target performance for "most areas".

It noted its performance in relation to water supply interruptions "deteriorated substantially" and, despite improving annual performance by 38%, said the company's total pollution incidents performance remained more than double its target.

Customer satisfaction also remained challenging, ranking 15 out of 17 in the sector.

While storm overflows performance improved by 19%, it still fell short of its target, the Environment Agency said.

It was, however, the only company to have met its target for internal sewer flooding, or how often wastewater enters a property, every year since 2020-21.

A spokesperson for South West Water said: "We are under new management with a renewed focus on improving our performance.

"We know there's much more to do and although it will take time, we are taking action and making progress in the areas that matter most to our customers and the environment."

They said the firm had "reduced spills from storm overflows by 17% last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%, and we have insourced over 40 new leakage specialists".

"We are working hard to build on the progress we're making, backed by record levels of investment across the region," the spokesperson said.

"We are transforming our network to improve long-term resilience of our water supply; protecting the environment and tackling leaks as part of our multibillion-pound plan to deliver the long-term improvements our customers and communities expect."

A separate report from the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat said South West Water's drinking water quality "remains exceptional, and consumers can be confident that their water is safe to drink".

It noted although its internal sewer flooding performance had deteriorated, "it is still performing better than the industry average".

However, it said overall environmental performance "is poor".

In a summary, the report said overall water supply interruptions "remain a significant concern, and it is one of the worst performers in the industry".

To improve the company needed to reduce interruptions and complete a transformation programme to address the root causes of its failures and "substantially improve customer interactions and overall experience", it said.

Surfers Against Sewage described the latest performance ratings as "another league of shame for water companies" but she added they were "a mere slap on the wrist that means absolutely nothing".

Head of campaigns Jo Morley said: "What is the point in these environmental performance ratings when year after year water company behaviour gets worse?"

articles.title: Rare beetle find in Gloucestershire shows species is 'on the move'
articles.summary: Scientists say the great silver water beetle has been found in areas it has never been seen before.
articles.body:
New sightings of one of the UK's rarest beetles shows the species is on the move, scientists say.

The great silver water beetle - which is usually found on the Somerset Levels and in the east of England - was spotted in two places in Gloucestershire - far further to the west of the country than usual.

Citizen scientists Gordon Kirk and Bill Watkins made the discoveries during routine moth monitoring in the Severn Vale and Beachley respectively.

Tina Bouttle, from Gloucestershire Centre for Environmental Records, said: "The great silver water beetle's conservation status is listed as near threatened. These are both significant records as it shows this species is on the move."

Despite looking black on land, when the beetle is in water where it predominantly lives, it holds a film of air against its belly which gives it the silvery sheen it is named after.

Bouttle said it was not yet known why the beetles were moving - although the team did have theories.

"We think that it's moving around the country looking for new wetlands as wetlands currently are suffering from pollution and habitat destruction.

"Or they just might be doing really well where they are and needing to find new places to move into," she explained.

Citizen scientists are members of the public who aid with scientific discoveries by - for example - monitoring wildlife around them and sending photos to scientific organisations to help identify them.

The People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES) promotes the importance of such volunteers.

"Citizen science drives so much of conservation and by reporting sightings to your local wildlife trust, environmental record centres or organisations like PTES, people across the country are helping to protect and better understand our wildlife," its conservation research and strategy officer David Wembridge said.

Members of the public are being encouraged by the Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust to become citizen scientists and submit beetle sightings to help track the biodiversity of the county.

"The majority of this year's records would have come from citizen scientists, so this shows you do not need to a professional ecologist to help towards the understanding of this species.

"Each record is a piece in the puzzle to understanding the movement of this species into Gloucestershire and beyond," Bouttle added.

articles.title: Northumberland Conservatives challenge Defra's Rothbury donation
articles.summary: The government is giving £1.9m to help conservation groups who are trying to buy a large estate.
articles.body:
Local Conservatives have challenged the government's £1.9m donation to help conservation groups buy a vast upland estate.

The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust are raising £30m to acquire the 9,500-acre Rothbury Estate in its entirety as part of plans to boost wildlife, restore bogs and promote nature-friendly farming.

But as the groups close in on the target , chairman of Northumberland Conservatives, Guy Renner-Thompson, said the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) should instead focus its support on "our farmers and fishermen".

Nature minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter said purchase of the site would benefit local communities.

Earlier this year, tenant farmer Chris Armstrong, who oversees 1,000 acres (405 hectares) close to the Rothbury site, told the BBC local opinion was split with most of the farming community seeing it as a "folly".

Renner-Thompson said the government had "its priorities wrong", referencing difficulties farmers had faced accessing sustainable farming incentive (SFI) funding.

"Defra should be focusing on its support of our farmers and fishermen, the people producing our food and sustaining Northumberland's rural and coastal communities," he said.

The Rothbury Estate sale has attracted support from the likes of Sir David Attenborough and the window for public donations is open until the end of the week.

If successful, the organisations claimed there would be the potential to develop a "40 mile nature recovery corridor stretching from the North East coast to Kielder on the central Scottish border".

Renner-Thompson challenged ministers to stipulate if any conditions would accompany the grant and how farmers and food production would be protected.

"We support investment that benefits nature and our communities," he said.

"But that does not put this particular purchase beyond scrutiny."

Riddell-Carpenter said: "This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to secure one of England's biggest and most wildlife-rich landscapes for nature recovery and for the benefit of local communities.

"That's why the government is stepping in to help The Wildlife Trusts secure the future of the Rothbury Estate, after thousands of members of the public pledged their support."

articles.title: Girlfriend’s family ties 31-year-old credit manager to tree, beats him to death with sticks in Gujarat after catching him with her
articles.summary: PALANPUR: A 31-year-old credit manager of a finance company was allegedly tied to a tree and beaten to death with sticks by his girlfriend’s family
articles.body: PALANPUR: A 31-year-old credit manager of a finance company was allegedly tied to a tree and beaten to death with sticks by his girlfriend’s family members after he went to meet her in Thangna village of Kheralu taluka in Mehsana district late on Wednesday night.Four people have been rounded up in connection with the murder, police said.The deceased, Ranjitji Thakor, was a resident of Vagharol village in Sidhpur taluka of Patan district and worked as a credit manager at Cholamandalam in Siddhpur.According to the FIR, he had been in a relationship with a woman from Thangna for about two years, and his family was aware of it. His first marriage ended in divorce in 2024, the FIR states.Ranjitji left home on his motorcycle for work around 9am on October 27. When his mother called him at 11.45pm, he reportedly told her that he would return late.Around 3.30am on October 28, a relative informed his family that he had gone to meet the woman in Thangna and had been caught by her family.The FIR alleges that the woman’s mother, brother and paternal uncle, along with another relative, tied Ranjitji’s hands and legs with ropes to a tamarind tree near their house and assaulted him with sticks.When he stopped responding, they allegedly placed him on a cot, where he died.Ranjitji’s father and other relatives reached the village around 9am after learning about the incident.They found his body on the iron cot beneath the tree, covered with a sack. The father told police that he noticed injury marks on his son’s back, neck, waist and legs. articles.title: South Korean prosecutors press for death sentence in Yoon martial law case
articles.summary: Former president faces renewed death penalty demand as he appeals life sentence for insurrection.
articles.body:
South Korean prosecutors are seeking the death penalty for former President Yoon Suk-yeol over his failed attempt to impose military rule.

The team led by special prosecutor Cho Eun-suk renewed the demand at an appeal hearing in Seoul on Thursday, arguing that Yoon’s actions threatened South Korea ‘s democracy.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment in February after being convicted of leading an insurrection.

Prosecutors had previously sought the death penalty at Yoon’s original trial in January, but the court sentenced him to life imprisonment the following month.

At Thursday’s hearing at the Seoul High Court, a prosecutor said there was “no reason to hesitate” over imposing the death penalty, according to South Korea’s Yonhap news agency.

South Korea retains the death penalty but has not carried out an execution since 1997.

Prosecutors argued that this long pause should not prevent judges from sentencing Yoon to death.

Yoon declared martial law on December 3, 2024, deploying soldiers and police to the National Assembly, South Korea’s parliament.

Lawmakers overcame a security blockade to vote down the measure, forcing the government to withdraw it about six hours after it was announced.

The lower court found that Yoon had tried to stop parliament from functioning, detain political opponents and remain in control of the country for an extended period.

Yoon’s lawyers told reporters on Thursday that he had intended to warn an opposition-controlled parliament against what he considered attempts to obstruct his government, not to establish authoritarian rule.

Speaking at the Seoul High Court on October 27, Yoon also denied seeking to establish a long-term dictatorship, according to the Hankyoreh newspaper.

The crisis led parliament to impeach Yoon in December 2024. South Korea’s Constitutional Court, which decides whether to uphold impeachments, removed him from office in April 2025.

The appeals court plans two more hearings, including Yoon’s final statement on November 5.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton says she regrets not dealing with 'reckless' Jim Comey in 2016
articles.summary: Hillary Clinton says she regrets not confronting James Comey over his actions as head of the FBI before the 2016 election, as new criminal charges loom over him.
articles.body: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton revealed during a podcast discussion on Wednesday that she regretted not confronting former FBI Director James Comey more forcefully ahead of the 2016 presidential election. "I wish somebody had told me that I needed to take on Jim Comey," Clinton said on "High Stakes" alongside Kara Swisher. "I needed to really challenge his breach of precedent, his breaking the Justice Department's norms of not interfering in elections, his deliberate, reckless effort to curry favor with the Republicans. I wish I had taken it on in a very forcefully, frontal way. And I didn’t." Comey, while serving as FBI director in 2016, sent a letter to Congress on Oct. 28, 2016 — exactly 10 years ago Wednesday — informing lawmakers that the FBI would review newly discovered emails potentially related to its investigation into Clinton's use of a private email server. Just two days before the 2016 election, on Nov. 6, Comey informed Congress that the review had not changed the FBI's earlier conclusion that criminal charges against Clinton were not warranted. HILLARY CLINTON INCLUDES 2016 LOSS IN 'HARD TIMES' LIST FOR DEM VOTERS, INCLUDING 9/11, 2008 FINANCIAL CRISIS "Did I want to pick a fight with the director of the FBI? Well, in retrospect, yeah, I did. So, yeah. I wish I had been, you know, really in his face and picked a fight with him in a way," Clinton added. Swisher agreed and said, "You have to push back." "I've been the do-right person for way too long when it comes to not fighting back, because you know the old assumptions are gone, and you've got to be much more in the mix and aware of, you know, what the real dangers are and speak up and fight back," Clinton added. The Justice Department filed criminal information against Comey on Monday over allegations that he willfully communicated national defense information to an unauthorized person in connection with an alleged 2016 disclosure. SECRET FBI PROBE CAST TRUMP AS POSSIBLE RUSSIAN ASSET AFTER COMEY FIRING, MEMOS SHOW Federal prosecutors filed the two-count criminal information in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging Comey communicated national defense information and conspired with others to unlawfully disclose it. The Justice Department said that the filing was made to preserve the allegations before the statute of limitations expired as an investigation remains ongoing. Prosecutors allege that on or about Oct. 5, 2016, Comey knowingly and willfully communicated information related to the national defense to a person who was not entitled to receive it. JAMES COMEY INDICTED FOR ALLEGED THREATS AGAINST TRUMP: DOJ FORMER FBI AGENT SAYS COMEY CHARGES HINGE ON INTENT EVIDENCE AND JURY INTERPRETATION Comey's attorneys have challenged the filing. They've argued that prosecutors cannot move forward with the case without first obtaining an indictment from a federal grand jury. Comey denied wrongdoing in an Instagram post Monday, calling the latest action an "appalling abuse of the Department of Justice." "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm not afraid of these people. And I still believe in the independent federal judiciary," Comey said. "To quote Elsa from ‘Frozen’: ‘Let It Go! Let It Go!’," Fox News contributor Joe Concha told Fox News Digital in a statement about Clinton's remarks. "As for Hillary, the way she so carelessly and recklessly, and probably illegally handled highly classified information is something she shouldn’t be revisiting now, as if she was the victim. Even if she took on Comey, that still doesn’t change the fact she never campaigned in Wisconsin. It doesn’t change the fact that she spoke down to more than 70 million Trump voters at the time whom she called deplorable. And it doesn’t change the fact that, without a time machine, she doesn’t get a do-over now." Fox News Digital reached out to Comey's team for comment. articles.title: Fighting rages near Yemen’s Taiz as UN urges humanitarian access
articles.summary: Fighting has forced more than 281,000 people from their homes in Yemen since the beginning of August, the UN said.
articles.body:
Fighting has escalated in Yemen, with media affiliated to government forces reporting a surge in hostilities with the Houthis on several fronts south of Taiz in southwestern Yemen.

Yemen Today TV reported on Thursday that fighting was taking place on the Al-Aqroudh and Al-Masrakh fronts, as well as in Al-Rahn village in the Sabir al-Mawadim district.

Houthi-affiliated media reported four air strikes against the city of Mocha and its port on the Red Sea, west of Taiz.

Yemeni government forces in Taiz said they repelled attacks on Al-Aqroud, as they tried to break the Houthi siege of the area.

“Our forces have carried out 749 military operations over the past 24 hours, resulting in the death or injury of 239 militants and the destruction of 117 vehicles and armoured vehicles,” Majid al-Nazili, a spokesman for Yemeni government forces, told Al Jazeera.

The Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – also advanced on Jabal Sabr on Sunday, the strategic mountain overlooking Taiz. It has become the focus of the fighting between the Iran-backed group and forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, backed by Saudi Arabia.

Meanwhile, flights have resumed at Aden international airport, the Anadolu news agency reported. Services were suspended on Wednesday after witnesses said a missile had landed on the Al-Nasr Camp, adjacent to the airport, where Yemeni coastguard forces and interior ministry headquarters are located.

A military source told Al Jazeera on Thursday that government forces carried out three air strikes against Houthi military gatherings and vehicles southeast of Taiz, claiming that they targeted the group’s positions and movements on the Al-Aqroud front. This comes as the Houthi group reported more than 100 air strikes targeting the capital city Sanaa, and eight other Yemeni governorates, over the past 24 hours.

The surge in fighting across multiple fronts in Yemen has worsened a spiralling humanitarian crisis .

The conflict has forced more than 281,000 people from their homes in Yemen since the beginning of August, according to the United Nations’ humanitarian agency.

The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that “time is running out” to deliver aid to the 800,000 people trapped inside the city of Taiz.

Humanitarian access has become increasingly difficult over the past three weeks, OCHA said, due to damage to a key road linking Taiz to southern governorates. Aid supplies now have to pass narrow mountain routes to reach people in need.

OCHA called on fighters not to target civilians or aid convoys. “All parties must respect international humanitarian law and allow safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access so that aid can reach people in need,” it said.

The war in Yemen has escalated sharply since the Houthis seized strategic territory from government forces along the Red Sea coast last month, prompting a counteroffensive. Saudi Arabia has since intensified its strikes on the group.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, which is aligned with Yemen’s government forces, have dealt a blow to the kingdom, the world’s biggest exporter of crude oil, disrupting its businesses, airlines and residents, and damaging its international image.

articles.title: 'Painful' years head, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
articles.summary: UK households face a drop in their disposable income over next three years, the Resolution Foundation is warning.
articles.body:
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.

The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.

But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.

"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.

However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

In response the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.

Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains made in the first five years.

Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.

The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.

Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.

The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.

The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.

Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay.

However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.

While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.

The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year.

"This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," added the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).

"No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."

IFS director Helen Miller said there would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament.

"Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said.

"Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.

Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.

Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.

He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.

Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.

But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" of the amount of buffer the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.

Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.
